speechtext: On the order for motions:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO RESULTS
speechtext:
I should like to make a brief statement with regard to the results of the sixth victory loan campaign.
Total sales of bonds amounted to $1,407,576,650. This represented 3,077,123 applications. These sales were made for payment in cash. The sixth victory loan did not involve the issue of any new bonds against the surrender of maturing securities.
It will be recalled that the total objective for the sixth victory loan was set at $1,200,000,000, and that this objective was split $525,000,000 for individuals covered by the general canvass and payroll savings canvass, and $675,000,000 for large investors, mostly business firms and corporations, covered by the special names canvass. Each of these objectives was exceeded by a wide margin.
Combined sales by the general canvass and payroll savings canvass amounted to $643,690,700, representing 3,070,601 applications. Sales in the special names canvass were $763,885,950.
The sixth victory loan attained new record levels in the total amount of bonds sold, in the total number of applications received, and in the dollar amount of sales to individuals covered in the general and payroll savings canvasses.
I should like to point out that applications by members of the armed forces form part of the figures I have given on sales to individuals. On the sixth loan, armed forces applications numbered 461,688 for $47,826,250 of bonds. Applications from overseas personnel of the armed forces, included in these totals, numbered 141,510 for $13,383,550 of bonds. All of these figures show a considerable increase over the results of the fifth victory loan. The record of support of victory loans by members of the armed forces, particularly from the men in the navy, army and air force overseas, is one of the most stimulating features of our victory loan campaigns. In supporting victory loans, the armed forces are showing their appreciation of the value of a reserve of savings for use
after the war. This evidence of their firm confidence in victory, and of their faith in the future of Canada, is an inspiration and an example to all of us on the home front.
These data have been compiled by the national war finance committee from information obtained at the time of public offering of the loans, and from other sources. The results of the sixth loan should be regarded as subject to revision when final figures with respect to this loan become available.
Costs of issue of the sixth victory loan, while incomplete at the present time, are expected not to exceed 88 cents for each $100 of bonds sold. Costs of issue on the first victory loan, in June 1941, were just over one per cent, but costs on all issues since that time have been less than one per cent.
With the consent of the house, I should like to place on Hansard for convenient reference a statement showing the estimated derivation of subscriptions to the sixth victory loan and preceding victory loans. All figures in regard to the sixth victory loan are subject to final verification on the receipt of reports of actual bond deliveries by banks, trust, and loan companies. The figures which I have used, and which appear in the statement I am placing on Hansard, are based on the final reports received in Ottawa from the provincial offices of the national war finance committee.
The following table shows the estimated derivation of applications for victory bonds at the time of issue of each loan.
The applications for each loan are divided into two broad classes, designated "Individuals" and "Non-Individuals".
The class designated "Individuals" includes two sub-divisions, described as "Special Names" and "General and Payroll Canvasses." The amounts shown for special names represent applications received in the special names canvass from individuals believed to be capable of buying $25,000 or more of bonds at the time of each loan. The amounts shown for general and payroll canvasses represent the combined total of applications received in these canvasses. General canvass applications include some sales to small commercial and small non-profit bodies. Total applications from these non-individuals would be a relatively small part of the total amount shown opposite the designation "General and Payroll Canvasses".

speechtext:
Hon. L. R. LaFLECHE (Minister of National War Services):	Mr. Speaker, may I
table copies of orders in council P.C. 5060 and 5061 of the 4th of this month. With regret may I say the first accepts the resignation of Mr. Rene Morin as chairman of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the second appoints Mr. Howard
B.	Chase to replace Mr. Morin.
May I explain that Mr. Morin has been connected with the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation since September 10, 1936. He consented to his appointment as chairman being renewed in November, 1942, but at that time he told me he could not give any guarantee that he would serve for the full period. Some time ago he intimated that his other duties had increased to the extent that he should tender his resignation as chairman. In doing so, he expressed appreciation of the staff of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and of his colleagues, and he was kind enough to say a word about the minister as well.
I am particularly pleased to be able to announce the appointment of Mr. Chase, which marks, I believe, some special recognition of labour. He has merited well of Canada and I know he will do so in his new appointment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a matter of privilege and as chairman of the parliamentary committee on radio broadcasting, I wish to make a brief observation based upon a press dispatch appearing in the Globe and Mail of July 6. The dispatch reads as follows:
Ottawa, July 5.-The parliamentary committee on radio broadcasting likely will recommend removal of the $2.50 licence fee, Douglas G. Ross, P.C., Toronto, St. Paul's, said to-day. The committee is currently in final session to draft recommendations to parliament.
This statement has been given wide publicity, and will no doubt receive further publicity. Let me say that the last two meetings of the radio broadcasting committee were held in camera; the statement issued did not emanate from the radio broadcasting committee and must be regarded as the personal opinion of the hon. member for St. Paul's.

speechtext:
On June 26 the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) stated, as appears in Hansard, page 4145, that it had been brought to his notice that on the closing of the A-4 training centre in the city of Brandon a large amount of surplus supplies were destroyed instead of being sold for salvage or turned over to citizens who could use them. I advised the house at the time that inquiries in the matter would be made forthwith.
I now want to say that a very full investi-[DOT] gation has been made. Statements have been received from officers concerned with the disposal of the supplies. Colonel W. G. B. Dailley, the chairman of the army salvage and disposal board, proceeded to Winnipeg and to Brandon, where he interviewed not only officers concerned but also a number of civilians who were mentioned as being critical of the manner in which the surplus supplies were dealt with.
The supplies disposed of were barrack stores consisting for the most part of earthenware, enamelware, and retinned mess-hall and kitchen utensils. All serviceable and nonserviceable stores which could be repaired or had salvage value were first gathered together and turned over to a central point for storage and shipment to ordnance. All stores considered to have no salvage value, such as plates, cups, saucers, enamelware, garbage pails, brooms, brushes, et cetera, were then gathered together in central locations throughout the camp for final inspection and disposal. They were then examined piece by piece by an officer and non-commissioned officers and a decision reached as to whether they were fit for further use or worth the cost of their return to ordnance in Winnipeg.
A total of 3,343 articles, having an original value of $2,169, were condemned and destroyed out of a total of 34,712 articles returned to ordnance by the units concerned, having a total original value of $45,338. This represented 9-6 per cent by number and less than five per cent by value. Approximately eighty per cent of the stores condemned and destroyed were enamelware articles, which had been condemned by the medical authorities.
The articles destroyed were put on the city dump and not sold as salvage because their value as scrap in the location where they were was considerably less than the cost would

be of the handling of them and the freight for their transportation to any place where they could be sold. The army authorities examined the articles carefully and took every precaution to save any which were reparable.
I should point out that articles which might appear suitable for civilian use on a cursory examination might nevertheless be properly condemned for military use under army regulations in the interests of the health of the troops, and of the health of civilians as well for that matter.
lam satisfied there was no breach of regulations or any waste of army property in the action taken at Brandon.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, July 5, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. L. Ilsley (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Rowe.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to refer briefly to certain clauses in the budget which to our group are objectionable, and in a general way to point out wherein the 1944 Canadian budget has failed to meet the needs of 1944 Canada, which is looking to the future.
It is just a month ago to-day that the allied forces swarmed across the English channel to the Cherbourg peninsula and there established themselves on what appears at the present time to be the prelude to victory. The price is being paid to-day, as it has been paid by Canada for a number of years. The constantly increasing lists of casualties which reach our desks daily keep Canada informed of the price she is paying-the price which the common people of this country are forced to pay in order to establish and maintain peace and a hope for the common man in the future of the world.
There are evident now some very broad shapes of things to come. Some of them are these. Among the victorious allies there is a determination that a return to some of the old things of the world as we knew it must never be permitted. The dead past cannot return. To-day the common man is on the march to a better world. It is only natural that this war should bring about some great changes in the thinking and demands of the people throughout the world. In the first place, we have to remember what the world has suffered in the past fifteen years-first, ten years of a devastating depression, and then five years of a devastating war. The impact of these two events upon humanity throughout the world, and the constantly improving conditions and facilities for communication between different parts of the world, must of necessity bring about some change in the thinking of people everywhere. We do not condemn the budget as a war-time measure in support of the war; we are all solidly behind it; but we do condemn its failure to look forward to the needs of the people of Canada who are and have been suffering for the past two decades.
The common man as he looks over Canada's budget in 1944 is impressed by one or two things. Number one is that he sees his pay envelope with fewer deductions from it, but

he knows that this means greater victory loans. One thing that does alarm him, however, is the constantly increasing national debt. We are not paying for the war. It will have to be paid for in the period that follows the war. Therefore we believe that this budget should have given some vision and some hope to the people that plans are being made now to make it possible for Canada to carry the load.
Prior to this war the national debt of approximately three billion dollars taxed the capacity of Canada's national income to carry it. Year after year we were borrowing money to pay interest on that debt. The debt was constantly increasing. I had hoped that the Minister of Finance, before he completed his discussion of the budget, would outline to the Canadian people what plans he has under the economy which he supports to take care of post-war financing the war and paying for it. Or are the Canadian people to expect a return to the excuses handed out to them following the last war? We are told that there is no money for social reform. "If you must enjoy the luxury of war, you have to pay for it." As one member of a delegation appearing before the reconstruction committee said, referring to paying for war, "If you are going on a spree, you must expect a headache to follow." We were told that we could not have security because of the great debt we had incurred. We feel that the budget of 1944 has failed because it has failed to meet that particular demand. The Canadian people are looking forward to something better than they had in the pre-war days.
What is the story of Canada? Seventy-seven years ago on July 1 last Canada was formed into a confederation. It was the richest land for its population, in the world. The comparatively few people in it have nearly half of the north American, continent with all its vast resources. The governments of this countiy were entrusted with the job of developing those resources-for what purpose? Surely the first purpose should be to supply the needs of the people in this land, to provide our people with the things that they require for decent living. Can anybody in this house maintain that they have succeeded in that? They have given away the resources of this country, largely to private industry, in many cases to monopolistic industry. All the Canadian people have asked is that they be given the opportunity to work in the factories and plants of industry to develop the resources, and in return for that labour be provided with an income with which they can supply themselves and their families with a decent living. In spite of the fact that these industries have our resources, large deposits of coal, nickel

The Budget-Mr. Castleden
and other minerals, the vast resources of waterpower, vast forest resources, the wealth of Canada from one end to the other, the economic organization of this country has failed to provide the Canadian- people with the bare requirements essential to enable them to attain a decent living standard.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is on a much higher level than that of any other country.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am making my speech now. I listened to you making yours and I did not interrupt. If I have time before my forty minutes are up I will permit questions from the hon. member.
Let us look at the 1944 budget and find out what has been done with regard to certain concessions to industry which operated in this country prior to the war. I refer hon. members to page 4181 of Hansard of June 26. I should like to read to the house a portion of the first paragraph on that page. It is as follows:
The proposal is that one-half the expenditure on maintenance and repairs, incurred in a period to be fixed by the governor -in council, may be charged against the income of a previous fiscal period but not farther back than the fiscal periods ending in 1943.
The next sentence is particularly significant:
In the case of the mining industry, maintenance and repairs will be held to include also underground development work.
With regard to income tax, that means the mining industry of Canada are going to be permitted to charge one-half of the expenditure of underground development against their income. Notice that the governor in council is given the power to determine the particular period. Order in council government has certainly reached dangerous limits in this land when the budget turns over to the governor in council the right to determine the period, and later on what particular areas, shall be affected with regard to oil development. This is the kind of thing which Canadians would do well to watch and curb.
The next paragraph affects practically all industries in Canada. This is what the budget says when referring to research work:
The classes of expenditure for research are not allowed as an expense of doing business: capital expenditures such as for laboratories, pilot plants, et cetera, and current expenses for research which are not directly related to the firm's immediate production activities. It is recommended that these limitations be removed and that all expenditures on research be -allowed in the year of expenditure and that research expenditures of a capital nature be written off as an expense over a period of three years.
In effect, that means that industry can carry on research and charge the cost of it back as a part of the expense of doing business, and thus reduce their taxable surplus. In other words, it means that to a large extent, the Canadian taxpayer is to pay for the research, but will get nothing out of it. Industry will gain all the benefits of the research. It will not be available to the people of Canada except that they have to pay through industry for the price of the commodity. It means that the benefit of scientific and technological development will go only to those who have the power to continue their exploitation of the- people.

I should now like to refer particularly to what is said about the oil industry. I refer hon. members to page 4183 of Hansard where the following appears:
The budget resolutions therefore include a recommendation to provide a tax credit of fifty per cent of the cost of any well drilled in the selected areas and spudded in between June 26, 1944, and March 31, 1945, if such well proves to be unproductive. speechtext: The tax exemptions are there, but the company makes the profit. It really means in the end, so far as such concessions are concerned, that private and in many cases monopolistic industry in Canada, dying of its own selfishness, now bleeds the public treasury to prolong its life and increase its power to exploit both Canada and Canadians.

speechtext: Do you object to the encouragement of oil production?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not think that the big oil monopolies of the world require any special concessions such as they have had in the past, particularly through orders in council of this government. Most of the oil companies are well able to take care of themselves. I do not see why special concessions should be granted to them. So far as this budget is concerned there is no indication as to whom the concessions are to go, to the small man or to the big man.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, you have reduced wages in Saskatchewan already.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are indications
that we have need of a budget which will provide for the economic and social welfare of the people before consideration is given to these rewards to capital. The health, education and well-being of the Canadian people should take precedence over the dividends paid to shareholders. Surely the Canadian economy can be so organized that our people will not be forced to stagnate under a system of private enterprise which recognizes no social responsibility and operates only to the extent to which it can extract profits.
The Canadian people were looking for something more than this in the budget of 1944. They were looking for something that would curb the powers of those people who in the past have done so well at the expense of the worker and the common man. The great Canadians of to-day should receive first consideration in any budget, and by great Canadians I mean those who have laid down their lives in this world conflict; I mean the wounded who are returning to us in increasing numbers; I mean the soldiers who have done their bit and are being brought back to this country; I mean the men and women in khaki, the fathers and mothers, the wives and sweethearts of our soldiers, some of whom have lost their dearest
'Mr. Castleden.]
and best in this war. I refer to the workers in the factories and fields, to the toilers who produce the wealth of the nation. What do those people want? What do they ask for to-day? Were the wants, the hopes and aspirations of these people in the minds of those who framed Canada's budget? I do not think so. Surely the sacrifices they have made deserve more than the hopelessness of the past, the low wage standards, the want, the slum conditions, the low educational standards, the denial to our young people of the right to live, the right which was denied them in the era to which hon. gentlemen to my right refer. Shall the Canadian people beg of industry the right to toil at low wages? Shall the farmer and producer continue to beg for a decent return for his products from monopolistic processors and those who purchase the products of their toil? Shall the consumer be compelled to continue to pay toll to those who control the very necessities of life?
The economy of Canada should be so arranged that there would be no scarcity in this land. Leisure could be used for recreational and cultural development.
Let me outline a typical project which might be undertaken at a time like this if there was any assurance that the necessary money would be forthcoming, that the economy of this land would be so changed that we could afford it. We have now something like 32,000 women in the armed forces of this country. When the war is over a large number of these women will be looking for a place in our economy. From that group of women we could develop a force of trained, experienced social service workers who could go into all parts of Canada and assist in instituting a health programme, in educating our people in the standards of nutrition; in carrying on cultural activities in various community centres; in bringing the story of our great Canadian national life to all parts of the country;, promoting national unity and giving people all over Canada an opportunity to give expression to themselves in the work they do. But if the 1944 budget is any indication, I am afraid Canada will not be able to afford that.
In this very city we have an example of what can be done in a democratic way by a group of enterprising people. I refer to a voluntary organization known as the Civil Service Recreational Association. Hon. members would be well repaid if they would take the trouble to look into what these people have done in order to enlarge the lives of those people who otherwise would be limited to humdrum office work. Now they have

The Budget-Mr. Caslleden
recreation; they have cultural activities; they have choirs and music; they have drama; they have sports and recreational activities of all kinds, almost one hundred in all. Many of them have discovered within themselves talents they never knew they possessed.
The Canadian people live to a great extent in frustration because of a lack of opportunity; throughout their lives they are forced to conform to a particular design, sitting behind a desk with no other means of expression.

The other day the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) said that the leader and members of this group had started something they could not control. In 1932 and 1933 this party started a truly democratic people's movement in this country. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is an example of the real, democratic operation of a party. Health, education and human welfare are to be the first aims and objects of the industrial, life and political organization of this country. If private profit prevents well-being,, then I say it should be replaced by a democratic and cooperative organization in society where service shall replace selfishness, as an expression of life.
May I say in closing that there are indications that the march of the common man is not confined alone to Canada, nor is it confined to the British empire. There is to-day the sound of the feet of the "common man" on the march, in his demand for a true recognition of the rights and importance of those who toil. It will not be denied. I condemn this budget as being reactionary. It may be Canada's last reactionary budget.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the remarks I wish to make this afternoon are suggested to me by three other speeches made in the house. I refer first to the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in introducing the budget, and next to the criticism of the budget by the nominated critic of the Progressive Conservative party. I should like also to make some observations upon the speech delivered a few days ago by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer).
The Budget-Mr. Maybcmk

I would say in the first place that, all things considered, in such times as these the budget is a good one. Pretty nearly everything possible by way of ameliorating conditions has been done-perhaps not everything, but the adjustments are many, and they are welcome. We cannot have, nor do I think we have any right to expect, a general lowering of taxation in war time.
Despite this truth it seems to me there is running through the speeches of members of this party sitting immediately to my left, the Conservative party, a longing, a sort of homesickness for the halcyon days of the last war, when wealthy men made large profits and did not pay much in taxes. Well, that sort of thing may be desired by some; but I am convinced that it is not desired by the rank and file of the people of Canada. We do not think that belts should be loosened at this time. With men bleeding and dying on the battlefields, in the air and on the seas we all know that the Canadian people cannot let up at this time; nor do they wish to do so.
Even in war time, however, there are some adjustments in taxation which can be made. Undoubtedly there has been pressure upon some people beyond what was just and equitable. An example will suffice to show what I mean. We had girl wage earners getting as low as $55 a month. If an increase were granted making $60 a month, taxation immediately stepped in and cut down that $5 to $1.50. In a year a $60 increase would be reduced to between $18 and $20. Absenteeism and damage to production were bound to result from that sort of thing. So that for practical reasons, as well as for the sake of justice, changes which should command approval have been made.
I say at once that I prefer to have an absolute exemption with respect to taxation, not an exemption such as we have at the present time which lasts only as long as a person does not have earnings above a certain stated amount. When we have a dividing line of that kind we are bound to get too great a spread between people on either side of the taxation exemption line.
Among the sixty odd changes which have been outlined in the budget speech, I think the one respecting alimony is worthy of attention. It is more important than would appear at first sight. Some of the injustices in the law as it stood were indeed simply outrageous. I know of a man who married a woman who had two illegitimate children. It was not very long before they added to the family, called "hers", some more children called "theirs." Then they were divorced, and he was ordered to pay alimony. Later he remarried, and there was more family.

Then came the taxes. Well, you can well imagine what happened. He was like the old woman who lived in the shoe, who had so many children she didn't know what to do. In his case it was that of having so many wives that he didn't know what to do; and also of having so many children that he didn't know what to do. On top of all, there were so many tax gatherers and so much taxes he was frantic. Everybody suffered. The budgetary proposal of to-day will remove such injustice, but it illustrates the nature of the change.
I now come to the criticisms of the budget offered by the Conservative party. I am bound to say that that criticism was well delivered. I remember hearing an old golfer speaking to another golfer who was looking for some praise in respect of his game. The old one said that the other fellow's stance was good That was as far as he would go. And so in this case I think we have to say that the critic of the Conservative party delivered his words of criticism in a very acceptable manner. So far, however, as the subject matter of the speech is concerned, the offering is entirely negligible. The speech was inconsistent, evasive and uncertain. Any positive suggestions are of decidedy small calibre.
So far as being evasive is concerned, let us take the position of that party on the subject of social security. In that respect they clearly evade the issue. The critic did pay some lip service to the general idea of social security. But all he offers, after opposing family allowances, is to set up a debating society to consider social security, to discuss it and to commune over it.
Their uncertainty of policy arises particularly in respect of their policy on manpower. The hon. member wants the men taken out of the army and put to work. Mr. McTague says that they should be kept in the army and sent to war.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I felt quite certain when the hon. member began, Mr. Speaker, that your ruling would be that there is no question of privilege. I am quite certain that I did not misrepresent what the hon. gentleman said, I listened to him with great care when he was speaking the other day and read his remarks afterwards. Perhaps he may not have had as much to do with the preparation of his speech as is sometimes the case with persons who deliver speeches, and he may have forgotten WThat its contents were.
Then with respect to the inconsistency of the hon. gentleman, first he placed his party squarely against the abolition of compulsory savings on the ground that he was opposed to inflation, but shortly afterwards he advocated a different form of tax reduction in the nature of exemptions. Obviously if there is inflation in the one there is inflation in the other. You cannot very well say that there is anything consistent about an hon. gentleman who at one moment says that you must keep spending power out of the hands of the people and keep this impost of compulsory savings upon them, and in the next breath say that you must put more money into their hands to spend by way of granting them a tax exemption.
I have said that his speech was well delivered, and I certainly stand by that; I do not want to go back on that-not one W'ord. But when you come to consider the matter which the speech contains, it is not any wonder that Mr. Bracken hid himself
away. Last year Mr. Bracken sat opposite his chosen financial critic and watched him and heard him perform. But this year, having doubtless had something to do with the preparation of the speech, it seems that he felt that he could not stick it. Consequently we had the spectacle of him avoiding his usual observation post across from his nominated chief critic and sitting away back in the farthest gallery almost hidden by a post. At that distance, far away from the eyes of the pitying people, he probably felt that his duty to his party could be made supportable.
So much for the criticisms of the financial critic of the Conservative party. At that, I have probably spent too much time upon it.
The exceptional oratory of the member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) holds every person, and it is not until one shakes himself free of the thrall of that oratory that some questions and doubts begin to arise in one's mind. I thoroughly enjoyed his speech the other day, but to-day I want to ask some questions and express some doubts.
The hon. member spoke of the national debt probably growing to $20,000 million and asserted that it would be unpayable and that the interest charges would crush us. The figure of $20,000 million is his guess, his estimate only. I consider the assumption a gratuitous one. Our experience in these very heavy war years hardly warrants the statement of such a figure. True, we are piling up debt, although we pay for a big share of our expenses as we go. Our total debt rose between 1939 and 1943 from $4,700 million to $11,300 million. It seems to me that recent events on the fighting fronts justify the belief that the end is not too far away, although certainly we have no justification for softening in our attitude towards the war. The figures I have mentioned, however, show that we have a long way to go to reach $20,000 million even if we keep up the rate of debt increase of the last few years. But the burden of debt is the interest that has to be paid. The total 1943 costs in interest were $304 million. The lower level of 1939 resulted in a cost of $169 million. In the interval-and indeed for some period before 1939-we were reducing the rate of interest. The rate was reduced between 1939 and 1943 from 3-61 per cent to 2-69 per cent. In other words, interest has not risen in proportion to the total of the principal of the debt.
We have no reason for fearing that such a load cannot be carried by the Canadian people. It is all wrong to try to make people frightened about their future. As a matter of
The Budget-Mr. May bank

fact, with practically all of this interest payable within Canada, the income of Canadians themselves is increased to the extent of $304 million. All this yields taxes. The actual interest load is not as great as at first sight appears.
The hon. member read a quotation from the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada, but he read only one sentence. I wish to read the whole paragraph, because it strongly supports what I have already said. That paragraph reads as follows:
In making these comments I do not wish to suggest that public debt could be increased at the present rate for an indefinite period without placing intolerable strain on our economy.
That is as far as the hon. gentleman read. Now I will read the remainder of the paragraph:
I do feel, however, that the war debt, and the increases which will inevitably take place for a time after the war ends, can be handled without serious embarrassment, The key to this problem, as to many others, lies chiefly in the maintenance of a high level of employment and income.
In saying that we probably would have $20,000 million of debt, the hon. member directed our attention to the fact that, immediately following the last war, expenditures were equally as high as or higher than they had been during the war years. It will help us to keep cool by recalling that expenditures right after the last war were expenditures made under conditions of a very serious inflation. The whole price structure was high, and naturally this was reflected in government expenses. High interest rates for war loans had the same effect. All this is different now, and there are many other different favourable factors.
The two things we have to guard against to protect our future are runaway inflation and a decrease in income through unemployment. Government policies have certainly been effective thus far with respect to inflation, and-this is something about which we cannot afford to take a chance. Our next duty is to make sure of the maintenance of a high income after the war. The Canadian people have no need to be timorous about this. With the great backlog of purchasing desire, with the millions of things to be done in this country, with the needs of the world outside this country, and with the strength of the postwar policies of this government, we can view the future of our country not merely with hope but with confidence.
I am not at the moment seeking to rule out the ideas of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. I could not do so until these ideas

are -clarified. I approach them, however, with caution particularly induced when I notice the use he makes of quotations. For example, the hon. member quoted a splendid and stirring passage from a speech of Field Marshal Jan Christian Smuts. I do not suppose that there is a man or woman in Canada who will disagree with what Smuts says are the needs of our situation with respect to social security and other matters. The field marshal is speaking upon an economic matter and the hon. member seems to approve the field marshal. Well, I find that his government, the government of South Africa, is financing along the same so-called orthodox lines as the Canadian government is financing, and as the British government is financing, and as most governments of the world are financing. The hon. gentleman must be a little extreme in his denunciation of the policy, in view of the fact that Smuts, of whom he approves does himself in turn approve the present day system.
But in this respect we can come much closer home. Another stirring, eloquent, inspiring passage has been read by the hon. member from an oft-quoted book of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). This is followed by a quotation from a speech which the Prime Minister made. Its most significant lines are as follows:
Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile.
The hon. member considers that to be sound economic doctrine. So do I. He holds the Prime Minister to be one who is deeply and keenly interested in the welfare of humanity; so do I. I think he further exhibits the Prime Minister as one who knows how, when opportunity offers, to effectuate his desires to improve the lot of mankind; so do I. Now this economic mind, the mind of the Prime Minister of Canada to which the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard pays tribute, is in favour of the present fiscal policy of Canada. The fiscal policy of Canada is his own policy. The taxation plans of this government and the victory loan plans of this government are his. This also was the case before the war.
I have difficulty then in following the hon. member when, in one and the same breath, he extols the Prime Minister with respect to his economic thinking as well as his emotional reactions, and denounces the Prime Minister's chief economic instrument as something which is utterly without health and no good at all. An all-out attack I can understand; and I can

The Budget-Mr. Maybank
understand full-throated complete approval; but kicking and kissing at the same time has never been comprehensible to me.
Not merely is there a need of clearing up such ideas as I have referred to, but I think the hon. member and those who believe with him. have to go farther and. have to clarify a number of points before we can give a proper examination to the supposed new monetary policy. I have listened to and enjoyed a great many of the hon. member's speeches, and yet I do not exactly know what he would have us do. Generally when he finishes a speech I find something in it which is suggestive of his plan, but I have never heard a complete and a precise and a concise disclosure by him. I note his condemnation of what he calls "unpayable debt," and I note that he flays the very idea of paying interest. But negation is not enough. Until he can get down to the point of writing his own idea of a budget speech, indicating what should be done respecting war expenditures and other expenditures, and all other details in connection with government financing, I shall find it impossible to follow him because I cannot tell where he will lead.
The nearest thing to any concrete proposal upon the subject of monetary reform which I have heard was the proposal of the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght). I do not know whether it can be justly termed the joint idea of these two hon. members, though it seemed to me that one did support the other. At any rate, to me that proposition did not look very good. It was, you will remember, a proposal that we print a billion dollars' worth of money-some such figure-or, if not print it, otherwise create it; it does not matter whether it be done with a fountain pen or with a printing press-and use this billion dollars for paying our expenses. I say it need not have been a billion; it could be more or it could be less.
All will admit, I think, that such a plan is not new. Various countries have tried it. It must be admitted, too, that it is not without benefit to some. To me it looks like a scheme which will enhance prices, and enhance them very greatly. This would benefit somebody. It would be a benefit to a man who has something to sell; that is, it would benefit him until he had to replace his goods. It would probably benefit large mine-owners; at any rate the wealthier. But for all people below the rank of the very wealthy it would mean disaster. A sharp upswing of prices would simply result in stark, unrelieved poverty for all except the very wealthy.
If I am wrong in claiming that such a policy means higher and higher prices, I
submit it is up to the advocates to show that I am wrong. This is another thing which has not yet been done.
I know it may be argued that by our controls we keep prices down at the present time and could continue to do so under such a proposed plan. But we do so, now, partly because we keep away from creating money in the manner of that proposal. Moreover, it is only because of the patriotism of our people for the prosecution of the war that controls work at all. If we should have to put up permanently with all the restrictions of to-day, life would not be worth living. There is no hope for all this fascist control in peace-time Canadian life.
Again I repeat that whatever the new budgetary policy is, it should be set forth clearly and, if possible, concisely. There is no hope of frank discussion until that is done. But in the meantime let us take stock calmly of our position and we shall know that we have no cause for fear. The Canadian people have met many complicated and difficult situations in their history, and they have not been worsted by any of them. All our history teaches us that we have a great destiny. We have evoked the admiration of every country in the world by the manner in which we have performed our tasks over the last five years. We have only to go away from home for a little while to find how good a place it is. Let us stop crying these horrendous tales of fear into the ears of people, making them uncertain about the future of the country. If there is a new money system which will make our life easier from now on, let us see it and let us learn all about it. No person is afraid to look. But there is no advantage in merely criticizing the system under which we have done the great deeds which we have done, and crying that it is all outmoded and outworn. In other words, there never was any advantage to any person in merely crying "stinking fish" on his own doorstep.
