speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two occasions during the session of parliament on which the private member has a little more latitude than usual. The debate on the budget is one of them. I am going to make a few remarks with respect to the budget, and I hope to keep within the ambit of the subject and not transgress the rules.
First, may I express appreciation of the difficult task which always faces the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) when he is preparing a war budget such as this. This is his sixth, and it is one of the largest budgets we have had. I believe however that the Minister of
The Budget-Mr. Perley

Finance is most sincere, and I trust that every other member of this house is equally sincere, in his desire to devise ways and means of raising the funds that are necessary to carry the war to a successful conclusion. And after that has been done we must also find the ways and means necessary for the reconstruction that is to take place in the post-war period so that we may have something worth while to which our gallant fighting men can return. We must win this war, and there is no question about it that we are winning it. I am sure every member was pleased to listen <jn June 29 to the speech delivered in this house by the Prime Minister of New Zealand, who made the definite statement that the war is in process of being won. He went further and referred to the gallant part our Canadian men and women have played in the different theatres of the war, and was gracious enough to express his appreciation of the part the Canadian people have played and will continue to play in supplying reinforcements for our men, munitions, food, and so on.
This budget will furnish those provisions. That is the purpose of it, and the government will no doubt find the necessary funds. I think that we are all agreed that any sacrifice that we on the home front can make, or which we have been called upon to make, is trifling in comparison with the sacrifices that our gallant men and women have been making on the fighting front. There are some outstanding features of this budget. First of all, the overall cash requirements will be $6 billion That is more than ever before by $200 million. Secondly, there are the borrowing requirements which are set out by the minister amounting to $3,200 million. That is $320 million more than last year's, and I have no doubt that in the borrowing process the minister will find the Canadian people as keen as they have been on previous occasions, and will have no difficulty in respect of the next loan. I have no doubt the next loan will go over the top. The compulsory savings feature has been eliminated. That represents $110 million, according to the minister's statement. It will mean, I believe, that the people will have that much more money to spend, and I think it is important that if they spend it they should buy bonds. If they do so, everything will be satisfactory. But if they use the money to buy other things, it may bring about the inflation of which the minister is so fearful, and he may have a little difficulty in that regard.
There is more for mutual aid by several millions. I am heartily in agreement with that, and I think that every member of the house endorses it. We all heard what the Prime Minister of New Zealand said; we

know what is taking place in connection with mutual aid supplies to Greece, and others of the allied countries, and it is all splendid. I am sure that every member of the house will be willing to support that feature of the budget.
There is an amount of $260 million for family allowances. I am going to wait until the resolution is before the house before discussing the question, but I might say in passing that I could produce letters which I have received from people not only in my own constituency but in other places in western Canada. However, I will leave that until we get to the resolution.
There is little change in the income tax; where there is, it will help those in the lower brackets, and we all agree to that. Some members, one to my left especially, have based their whole speeches on the fact that farm implements are to be put on the free list. I am free to say that this may help, and it should be a help with the experience that we have had with our neighbours to the south during the war itself. I support it as far as it goes, but how far will it go? I may say to the minister that unless the import quota restriction on farm equipment is removed it will be of little value. However, there are some features of this m-atter to which I would call the attention of the house. First there is the ten per cent war exchange tax which is to be removed. It is a war measure, and that is all right. Then there is the seven per cent duty which is to be removed, and that is an act of parliament that could be undertaken at any time. Both these are levies at the border where the goods come in on the basis of the retail price, which is nine per cent over the wholesale price, and that should be taken into consideration.
I would point out that the total farm business in implements in Canada, both imports and domestic, shows that tractors form sixty per cent, while the total imports from the United States of implements show fifty-two per cent as tractors, coming in free of duty now. Bear that in mind. The total business, domestic and import, is sixty ' per cent tractors, and fifty-two per cent of the imports come in free now. Take the other forty-eight per cent of the imports of implements into Canada and you find that some of them bear a seven per cent duty, some three per cent, some nothing at all, and the average is 314 per cent duty. What will the farmer pay? Anyone can get the figures from the bureau of statistics. The farmer spends on the purchase of implements only three and three-fifth cents out of every 100 cents he pays out in farm expenses. How much will he pay on

The Budget-Mr. Perley
the forty-eight per cent that comes in from the United States when the duty is three and a half per cent? Let me reduce this matter into the language of the farmer. Take wheat. The farmer averages net $1 a bushel. There is a ceiling of 11.25, but he averages now practically $1.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is no ceiling at all.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, $125; that is the set price. Now, on one bushel of wheat how much will the farmer save? The duty being three and a half per cent, if out of every $1 of his expenses the farmer spends 3-6 cents on implements, on a bushel of wheat, that is a dollar's Worth of wheat, the saving, will be one-eighth of a cent. Therefore, if a farmer spent the returns of one thousand bushels of Wheat on implements coming into Canada, what would he save? Under this budget he would save exactly $1.25. Hon. members can figure it out for themselves.
In a few respects I do not think this budget gives enough consideration to the chief industry of. agriculture. True, as the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) said, the three primary industries of agriculture, mining and forestry provide the major portion of our national income. But, Mr. Speaker, I would say that agriculture is the chief one. When it is considered that one-third of our population are either on the farms or are interested in farming, and a review is made of the portion of the national income that they have received over many years, it will be found that they never received more than fifteen per cent, and in many years much less. The reason I am speaking as I am to-day is that no one can properly represent a constituency in Saskatchewan or in western Canada who does not centre his attention on agriculture. It is our chief industry. Relatively speaking a very small percentage of the funds which are to be raised by taxation under this budget will go to agriculture. We are not complaining about the amount required to win the war. Therefore, in many respects I support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. So far as the amendment affects the farmers I think it is very good.
I agree with what the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) said, namely, that the farmer's income should be averaged over 6ix years. Last year the minister said he was agreeable to three. I remember the discussion that took place. On that occasion I suggested it should be longer. I am quite frank in saying that I would go farther than
either the amendment or anything that has been done by the government. I would exempt the farmers from taxation altogether.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. members may laugh, but I shall tell them why I make that statement. I say that there is no industry in Canada that has had more years of operation that show a loss. There is no industry in Canada that is operated under more hazardous and difficult conditions than farming. If hon. members will review the income statement they will see that in the year 1942 only 1,488 farmers paid a tax, and it was the paltry sum of $100 apiece. I say, why bother with them at all? Give them some encouragement.
May I quote what I said last year, and which' I wish to repeat to-day? Speaking on the budget on March 15 of last year I said, as appears at page 1239 of Hansard-.
I am going to offer a suggestion with respect to these farm incomes, because the tax collected really does not make it worth while 'bothering 750,000 farmers. I am going .to suggest that the farmer, especially the farmer of western Canada, be allowed to charge as part of his operating cost a fair wage paid to his wife and daughters and young sons who help him on the farm. I am going to ask that every farmer in Canada be given exemption from the payment of income tax unless he can show $2,000 of a net income.
That is what I suggested last year. The proposed amendment of this year goes pretty nearly that far, but not far enough. I would go farther, and as I said in my final suggestion last year, I would exempt the farmer.
I now come to the important question of floor prices. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is not in his seat. He sent me a note saying that it was impossible for him to be here. I appreciate that. On Friday last I asked him a question with respect to the introduction of the bill providing for floor prices. He said that it was being prepared and would come down in due course. I say we should have had it when it was first suggested that it would be brought in. We should have had it at least two months ago, and we should be considering it along with the budget. When we get it I hope it will contain a price that is at least parity. I do not know whether hon. members know what parity means, the word has been used so often. We now have a ceiling price on farm products that is out of all reason. So far as wheat, oats and barley are concerned it should be a price comparable to that which is received net by our United States cousins; it should be comparable to that which the

The Budget-Mr. Perley

The third paragraph is:
That no provision 'has been made to encourage greater war-time production by exempting overtime pay from income tax.
I believe there is nothing this government could do which would have a greater effect in stimulating the production of material and equipment for vrar purposes.
The next paragraph states:
That sufficient provision has not been made for the elimination of the inequities presently existing with respect to agricultural taxation.
I believe I have endeavoured to make myself clear on this point. Certainly I agree with that paragraph.
With respect to the simplification of the income tax form, I know that many people are confused beyond all measure. I myself have been confused. AVhen making out my form I had to go down to the Ottawa office, and, I am frank to say, the officials down .there did not know as much about it as did those out in Regina, where I finally got it *straightened out.
I shall not take more time of the house. It has been my purpose only to bring a few matters to the attention of hon. members. I could have said much with respect to soldier settlers' debt, but the house knows where I stand on that point, because I advocated two years ago that the minister would have been .away ahead if he had written it off.
I shall not discuss banking, because that *matter has been discussed to some extent in committee and in due course will be the subject of discussion in the house. I shall reserve for the committee stage anything further I have to say. I hope then to be able to discuss in greater detail one or two points to which on this occasion I have made little more than a passing reference.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first congratulate the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Lapointe) upon the fine sentiments he has expressed, and his just pride in the members of the armed forces
IMr. A. J. Lapointe]
from his constituency who are serving overseas. I have some knowledge of the part of the country he represents, and it deserves all that he says of it. It is a beautiful country. Before saying much about the budget I wish to take exception to some remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer). On several occasions he has said in this chamber that conditions between 1930 and 1935 were the responsibility of the government of the day. I would remind him and the house that if any government were responsible for those conditions it was the Liberal administration which held office between 1926 and 1930. They laid no plans to withstand the results of world-wide depression, stimulated! by intense nationalism and accompanied by falling prices. As a matter of fact they did not even know in the early part of 1930 that there was any unemployment. That same year a Conservative government took office and found that no preparations had been made by its predecessor to meet the terrible situation which then confronted the country. Let me point out that Mr. Bickerton, speaking before the banking and commerce committee, said that Mr. Bennett provided the mechanism Which helped to. take the country out of the chaos it was in at that time. Mr. Bennett and his government were responsible for the establishment of the Bank of Canada; and Mr. Bickerton of the Federated Association of Agriculture gave great credit to that government, remarking that he did not know how this country would function at the present time had it not been for what Mr. Bennett's government did.
Our first responsibility to-day is to win the war, not only against the nazis but against the Japanese. We do not know how long it will take to do that; the time may be short or it may be long. One thing is certain, that all the money which will be required to finish the job will be willingly furnished by the people of this country. Our armed forces will not be let down, if Canadians have anything to do with it, through lack either of supplies or of reinforcements for overseas. As far as our own party and I myself are concerned we shall do our best in spite of everything to see to it that these supplies and reinforcements get overseas to our troops.
There is to-day great fear on the part of our people. They believe that the government is doing no more planning for the future than it did in the past. No wonder there is distrust and unrest. That is what is troubling our armed forces; they do not know what will happen to them when they come back.

The Budget-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
The government has always been so full of indecision that there is much distrust in the minds of the people.
The speech from the throne is mere windowdressing; it contains all or nearly all the accumulation of progressive legislation which should have been introduced during the past nine years. The government displays the same old policy of drift and the same reluctance to do anything for fear a vote or two may be lost. So far as my observation goes the government has never done anything unless it has been forced to do so by the official opposition. For us this is a matter of pride. Evidence of its truth was furnished by a former Minister of Public Works, the hon. member for Richelieu-Yercheres (Mr. Cardin). He has not changed his mind, I believe, on that point.
One could not help noting that many of the policies adopted by our party at the Winnipeg convention have been included in the speech from the throne. Provision for some of them will be found in the budget, and I congratulate the ministry upon that fact; it shows good judgment. It requires some outside force to give leadership to a government whose policies ever since 1919 have never indicated any element of leadership. Their pre-election policies appear in the speech from the throne and -now-in the budget. Throughout its wartime administration the government has had one eye on the war and the other eye on the ballot box. It has shown the same old reluctance to deal positively with matters of importance unless forced to do so, the same unwillingness to accept positive, constructive criticism from the opposition or from the public. Now that it is in need of a bait for the election, there are dangled before the people many illusory lures in the hope that they will attract some votes on this political fishing expedition. Also, in the dying days of this government, in this last and most decisive year of the war-or so the minister has told us, and we believe it-they right-about-face on the policy against inflation. This is the year of the largest expenditure in Canadian history, the year when there has been a greater demand for workers than was ever known before. The government have caused all these welts and bruises to the people of Canada by raising the bogey of inflation and committing many other mistakes. They have created dissension by their determination to fight a Liberal war; and, because the welts and bruises have not been laid on impartially, but have always been the result of political expediency, the public is resentful.
Take the enforcement of national selective service. If it had been enforced impartially on all, the people would have stood for it
willingly; but when it is imposed rigidly on the willing horse in some parts, and otherwise on the unwilling, the willing horse of course resents the discrimination. However, in spite of all that, the people of this country have responded magnificently. Our voluntary enlistment has been splendid, but our call-up system has been a farce. It has not been enforced impartially. When one speaks of partiality and impartiality, can anything be more partial than the singling out of certain articles of consumption such as beer, liquor and wines? Is there impartial administration there? Why were these articles singled out to be rationed by the provinces? Why was not gasoline rationed in that way? Why was not sugar or cigars or cigarettes or tobacco singled out to be rationed by the provinces? Why should rationing be under the auspices of the provinces with all the discrepancies that have taken place in the meantime and the disunitj' that has been caused in this matter? I will tell you. When all the other rationing was done under the auspices of the War Measures Act an exception was made in this case, because it was obvious on the face of it that there was too much political dynamite in it, and therefore the buck was passed to the premiers of the provinces. There were too many circular letters from prohibition advocates. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was afraid to face the issue, and so he escaped responsibility by putting it on the shoulders of the provincial premiers.
Our factory workers have done an admirable job not only in the factories but outside in their spare time, and our white-collar workers have also done very well indeed. Despite hardships and trying circumstances under which they have had to carry on, they have endeavoured to keep the places open for the boys who will be coming back from overseas. Many white-collar workers in my own city have been offered jobs elsewhere at higher salaries, and their salaries have been frozen. They could go over to the government departments, however, and get an increase, but in spite of that they have stuck to their guns because they wanted to help the boys who have gone overseas. Our business men also have done a wonderful job and have given freely of their time. Our farmers, too, deserve a great deal of credit. Their production has been enormous. The people's subscriptions to the victory loan have also been admirable. As the minister pointed out to-day, our effort in this regard has been magnificent. When we consider that $1,407,500,000 vras raised in the last loan, it shows that our people will rise to any occasion for a good cause.

The Budget-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
Our armed forces have been magnificent. They have had to sustain hardships and tedious waiting. Many have been away for a long time, and that is something else that I have already spoken about, because I could not see why we should retain here a home army who had nowhere to go while we have had those boys over there all these years. They might have been easily relieved by some of these 70,000 men, who could have given them a chance to get back. It is a little late now, I suppose, to urge this once more. However, our troops overseas have covered Canada as well as themselves with glory. They have made a name for this country in the world, a name which will live forever; we must never forget. But all these things have been done in spite of frustration and lack of full leadership simply because the government has had one eye on the war and the other on the ballot box.
The people have responded to regimentation and regulation. With some of the budget proposals I agree and, while I do not want to go into details, I will mention, in passing, relief from the savings portion of the tax, certain relief in connection with medical expenses, relief in connection with the blind, married persons separated, allowance for fulltime housekeeper, superannuation and pension fund, payments to trade unions, relief for business to help full-time employment so that business can plan, and so on. But many of these things have been advocated before by His Majesty's loyal opposition. All through the war the opposition have advocated many of these and others as well. Take, for instance, the tax deduction for guest children. Repeatedly this government has refused to do anything in this regard, on some technicality or another, except in a few instances. Take the deduction in connection with illegitimate children, in-laws and alimony. Were these suggestions given consideration by the government? No. The public must grin and bear it because they had to be reserved as bait for the electors on the approach of an election.
Has the government policy with regard to anti-inflation been altogether sound, or has it militated against production?. Has it ground down the workers in the lower brackets below the actual decent cost of living standard in many cases? Has it not been very difficult to get any relief under these circumstances? There are many illustrations of the manner in which this policy has militated against the decent standard of living of many of our workers, more especially those who were not in essential war work or who were not in a position to do war work.

Comparisons have been given by the minister to show our taxation and the taxation in various other countries. Comparisons, of course, are odious at any time and more particularly in this case, because a comparison of taxation in other countries with taxation in Canada cannot be made unless we have the full gamut of all the taxes that are to be taken into account, both direct and indirect, provincial and municipal, and more so when we consider the cost of living in Great Britain and Australia, for example. These are compared from time to time, but you cannot make comparisons with Australia, New Zealand and Great Britain. The food may be the same or it may be different; clothing may be the same; but there is one item, more important than others as far as Canada is concerned, and that is fuel to keep Canadians warm in the winter. That has not been taken into consideration. When these cost-of-living indices are given to the people showing that this has gone up so much and the other has gone down so much, you cannot compare the cost of living in Canada with the cost of living in other countries. We have a severe winter in Canada. What family in this country can get by, even in the poorest circumstances, with less than 8100 a year for fuel to keep them warm? And there are other circumstances that must be taken into account in a cold country. There is greater expense in connection with clothing; there must be more food and different kinds of food as well as more expensive food, and then there is the question of sickness. When there is sickness in Canada it takes a person longer to get better. All these things enter into the picture. One could go on at great length enumerating different items that enter into the cost of living.
Now, leaving that for a moment, another proposal of our party which has been conceded by the government is that of relief to business in the form of allowing reserves to be built up for the post-war years. There is no difference in that. The relief is there. That is to say, businesses will have an opportunity of planning for the future so that they will not go broke in the years when business is not good. If this relief were not given and they ran into a bad time they would be forced to put hundreds and perhaps thousands of their workmen out of jobs.
A great deal has been said about compulsory savings being a nest-egg and a hedge against inflation. What effect will the abolition of the compulsory savings portion of the tax have on a family in the low income brackets in so far as post-war security is concerned? The government knows as well as I do that the small

The Budget-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
amount they will have saved1 up by that time will be a mere pittance and will not amount to anything. If the government wishes to do something for the low wage-earner and the people who are in poor circumstances, let them come out frankly and forget about this talk of inflation in connection with the low wage-earner. Let them come out frankly and lift up the exemption on the single man to $800 and on the married man to $1,500. After the low wage-earners have fed and clothed their families and paid their rent, the amount they will have to spend would not mean anything. As far as affecting inflation is concerned it is just the same old bogey.
The whole object of the government seems to be to keep these poor people frozen at low levels, people who are unable to make wages that are in any way comparable with those made by others on war-time jobs. If we want to be fair about this thing what we should do is put a proper floor under wages so that every person in the country would have a decent standard of living. The government have been propounding, and rightly so, their anti-inflation policy. In many respects I agree with them, but as far as the low wage-earner is concerned it seems to me that the government have built up a house of cards only to knock it down. I do not think it is necessary in this case to think so much about inflation.
The controls we have had on consumption goods have been good, although I believe they have been fairly strenuous at times. The people of Canada are quite willing to obey the law. They have a great sense of responsibility with regard to these matters, but you cannot tell the man in the low wage brackets that the few extra dollars he is going to get are going to raise blazes in this country as far as inflation is concerned.
With regard' to the compulsory savings portion of the tax, the people had no faith in the fact that it belonged to them. They had nothing to show for it. It was just considered as a tax. I think the people of Canada will supplement a portion of the compulsory savings tax andl buy victory bonds and stamps far in excess of what they did before, and they would do better than that if the exemptions were raised a little.
With regard to anti-inflation the government's policy has, in the main, been sound. Has it militated against production? I say here and now that it certainly has. There has been no leeway in the matter, and when it comes to asking a workman to work overtime in one of those war factories he says, "What is the use; the government gets it nearly all?" Why is this answer so prevalent? Well, I will tell you. He sees hundreds of
workmen idling around in factories with nothing to do. When the veterans of the last war and the great many other men who are past military age see young men in factories being, transferred from non-essenial jobs to essential jobs to get postponement and knows also that the home army is costing the country $150,000,000 a year; when he knows that in the neighbourhood anywhere up to a quarter of the employees in a factory could be utilized in other jobs, why should he work any longer or harder for very little or nothing? There is no patriotic spirit aroused, and I do not blame him. He sees there are lots of people in the factory who would have less to do if he worked longer than a certain length of time each week. Is this an anti-inflation policy, to have a quarter to one-third more employees in a factory earning high wages and more leisure time in which to spend the money? Certainly the greatest caution must be exercised in the prevention of inflation, but the method used in connection with factory workers seems to the people to defeat its own purposes.
In passing, may I say this further word? One of the reasons for the distrust and unrest among so many people in Canada is that the war expenditures committee is sitting in camera behind closed doors. The public well know that many matters which they have been investigating have very little bearing on the question of the war or of giving comfort to the enemy. I know of only two or three matters that have been dealt with by that committee, one of which was the shoe contract. How could that have anything to do with giving comfort to the enemy? Another one was the purchase of the Gimli airport. How could that have anything to do with giving comfort to the enemy? I do not know whether these contracts were right or wrong, but the point is they were investigated in secret. As a matter of fact the public have a right to know how the money has been spent, and if there is anything wrong they have a right to know that. There is no doubt that there has been waste and that it has been unavoidable, but again there have been extravagances which could have been avoided. Nobody blames anybody for justifiable and honest mistakes. They are bound to occur, but no one can say that there have not been many made. An explanation could easily have been given for many of these matters, but these in camera, behind closed doors, star-chamber sittings of the war expenditures committee have cast a veil of suspicion over the minds of the public in general.
May I now say just a word about the best possible man-power policy of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell)? The function



The Budget-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
of national selective service is to transfer workers to vacant jobs. On June 13 Mr. MacNamara, director of national selective service, announced that there were 202,323 job vacancies other than in logging or farming for 134,000 men and 67,323 women. Now, just think of the incongruity of the statement issued by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics when they announced that 14,095 men and women-and I might say that this is three times the number for last year-had unemployment benefits during the month of May I Not only that, but they averaged seventeen compensating, unemployed days apiece. Think of that, plus nine waiting days' time which must elapse before the benefits can be paid! This makes a total of 366,470 man and woman days not only lost to the production of the country, but paid for in unemployment insurance.
Another matter with which I wish to deal is the question of housing. Ever since I have been a member of this house I have appealed to the government in connection with conditions in my own city. I have had some success, but very little. Part 2 of the housing act has never been brought into force; that is the part dealing with low-cost housing. It is true that part 1 of the act has been in force and has been of great benefit to home owners, but it has not helped those in the low income brackets, the people for whom some provision must be made. They are the forgotten men. The .home improvement plan has done some good; to a limited extent it has improved the lot of the low wage-earner. Some old houses in the slum sections of my city have been fixed up; but this has not helped the children, for these are still slum areas, and the conditions under which these children have to live has resulted in a great increase in juvenile delinquency. Perhaps on another occasion I shall have more time to deal with this question of low-cost housing, -but another lure has been dangled in the political fish-pond by the government, which purports to intend to do something about low-cost housing. We shall have to wait and see what happens. All these years have gone by and the people of my city have had to grin and bear it. I have in my hand to-day's issue of the Globe and Mail, containing an article dealing with this matter, which reads in part as follows:
Eviction orders were refused, or stays of execution of such orders were granted, thus leaving many families in the premises they occupied

and thus, -also, tying up an indeterminate series of moves -by other families who were automatically frozen when one in the link of moves was -una-ble to provide vacancy of the premises.
Since that d-ate all of the months of May and June have -passed and July is on its way to antiquity-and the situation is becoming more
EMr, Douglas G. Ross.]
serious because of this factor, according to Miss Dorothy Dennison, director of the housing registry. People were able to take temporary refuge in summer cottages, tents and hastily erected shacks. When -fall conies, however, they have to seek -permanent quarters, and Miss Dennison estimates that there are hundreds of families in this plight.
At the present time some 1,900 families are on the Toronto housing registry. The situation is very serious. The home conditions of workers in certain sections of my own riding, as well as in other sections of the city, are very bad; they were slums before the war, and certainly they are worse now. I have brought up this matter on the floor of the house time after time; I even read one of the many telegrams I have received. I was almost ashamed to read it, to show the terrible conditions that existed in my own riding: vermin-infested; overrun with rats; families of four, five and six living in one or two rooms, not from choice but because they have no other place to go; overcrowded parts of the city still more overcrowded. Conditions were bad before the war, but with the influx of people to the city the situation has become intolerable. The only answer we have -been given is, "Why should the federal government look after Toronto?" I suppose it is on the same old basis as the famous speech made years ago by the Prime Minister, when he did not know there was any unemployment in the early part of the depression, and when he said he would not give one five cent piece to Tory Toronto. I brought the matter of the eviction of soldiers' wives and families to the attention of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), but his answer was that he did not see what he could do about it. The mayor and board of control of my city have come to Ottawa in an attempt to get some action, and I give them great credit for what they have done. We interviewed many of the ministers, but were given t.he same old answer; Toronto was turned down.
After all, Mr. Speaker, whose responsibility is it? What brought about this situation? The people employed in plants ten or fifteen miles from the centre of Toronto had no place to live but the city. Some fifty or sixty- thousand workers in the surrounding district were overlooked and forgotten by wartime housing; no provision was made to enable them to live near their plants. It is a strange anomaly when we have the government on the one hand asking the workers to live near their plants, for the sake of efficiency, and at the same time saying that the city of Toronto must take care of them. Very little has been done in the Toronto vicinity by wartime housing. I believe some six or seven hundred houses were

The Budget-Mr. McNevin
put up near Long Branch, which is fifteen or sixteen miles from Toronto, and some others were built at Pickering, which is twenty-five miles away. Other cities, such as Hamilton and Montreal, have been treated differently; wartime housing saw to it that accommodation was provided near the factories, in order to relieve the congestion in those cities, but not so Toronto. Think of the time it takes these people to travel back and forth every day. At a rough estimate they lose upwards of two hours a day to get to and from their work. I know of cases where people have to get up around four o'clock in the morning in order to get to their work at these plants. The transportation commission has done a wonderful job in trying to take care of them, but when we have such a scarcity of gasoline why should we have to waste thousands of gallons in order to transport workers ten or fifteen miles each way every day, instead of building these houses near the factories? On July 4 the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Chevrier) dangled some more political bait before the electors, when he said the government had consented to build a few wartime houses in Toronto, but they are not to be for workers; they are to meet the requirements of soldiers' wives and children. Of course that is vitally necessary. I could read letters I have received from Mrs. N. Hall Humpherson, president of the Soldiers' Wives Association, in which she points out that the housing registry has received some 1,700 applications for accommodation for wives of men serving overseas. The situation as far as they are concerned is appalling, and I hope some relief will be given.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, in order that the record may be complete, I should like to read the amendment moved by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). It was as follows:
(a)	that no adequate steps have been taken to simplify the forms and modernize the methods of taxation;
(b)	that no effective action lias been taken to grant a measure of relief to the men and women in the lower income brackets by raising the exemption in income tax for single persons to not less than $800 per annum and for married persons to not less than $1,600 per annum.
(c)	that no provision has been made to encourage greater war-time production by exempting over-time pay from income tax;
(d)	that sufficient provision has not been made for the elimination of the inequities presently existing with respect to agricultural taxation;
(e)	that no adequate provision has been made to ensure increased post-war employment through the discovery and development of metallic and noil-metallic mineral resources;
(f)	that the government has failed to make effective the full mobilization of our financial, industrial and material resources, as well as our .man-power, but is maintaining a so-called home-defence army, at a cost to the taxpayer in excess of $150,000,000 per annum, at a time when the need for men for army reinforcements, for farming and for industry is so urgent.
I am heartily in favour of all those paragraphs in the amendment. Time will not permit my saying much about them at the present time, but when the resolutions are in committee I shall have an opportunity to do so.
There is no doubt about this being primarily a pre-election budget, When it is fitted into all the rest of the jigsaw puzzle of the government's proposed legislation, it will show that the bait is being set in the political fishpond to catch the many and various classes of voters.
My chief criticism is that all this proposed legislation should and could have been enacted years ago. The government has been callous in' letting the people bear unnecessary suffering in the past, in order that it can now take the position of solicitously administering to their relief-and this just before an election. But by this time the people of Canada have had enough experience to say, "Once bitten, twice shy." They will look before, they leap. My warning is: Beware of the Grits, when they come bearing gifts.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget debate is an occasion which offers a wider scope for discussion of public questions than is afforded by ordinary items in committee. I should like first to make a suggestion of an expenditure which might be considered for the post-war period and which has a bearing on the riding I represent. I suggest that assistance be granted in establishing at least the smaller type of airfields. The constituency I represent is one of our great tourist areas, a magnificent playground, but the resources of our people are not sufficient to provide landing facilities for the smaller or civilian type of aeroplane. There is ample water for landing seaplanes, but of course the seaplane is a plane that is too large for the average citizen. I believe that if assistance were given not only in this area but in other areas to establish such landing facilities, it would pay ample dividends in the years to come.

The Budget-Mr. McNevin

Coming more directly to the budget I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) upon the removal of the ten per cent income war tax on farm implements and upon placing these implements of production on the free list. I think it was the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) who suggested this afternoon that this item was of very little importance. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have been associated for a substantial period of my life with farm organizations, and I do not recall a single instance when representatives of these organizations were presenting their views to succeeding governments when they did not press for farm implements being put on the free list. Our farmers for more than a decade past have continually pressed to have the implements of production put on the free list and now their objective has finally been realized.
I think it was the same hon. member who *suggested that the amount involved in this item would be very small indeed. I turn to the appendix to the budget to demonstrate that all the implements put on the free list are of substantial importance. I shall refer to a few of them.
First, there are cream separators and complete parts therefor, including steel bowls. They are now free under the British preferential tariff and under the intermediate and general tariffs. Previously the intermediate and general tariffs on the goods covered by this item carried a duty of ten per cent, so that here there is a ten per cent reduction.
Then take item 409a: milking machines and attachments therefor; centrifugal machines for testing butterfat, milk or cream: complete parts of all the foregoing. These are now free under all tariffs. Previously this item carried a ten per cent duty.
I now come to the more general list of farm implements found in 409b: cultivators, harrows, seed-drills, horse-rakes, horse-hoes, scufHers, manure spreaders, garden seeders, weeders, and complete parts of all the foregoing. They are now free under all tariffs. The intermediate tariff on goods covered by this item was formerly 7i per cent. The general tariff was twenty-five per cent.
Then item 409c: ploughs, farm, field, lawn *or garden rollers: soil packers, complete parts of all the foregoing. They are now free under all tariffs. The intermediate tariff on goods covered by this item was 7\ per cent and the general tariff twenty-five per cent.
Then item 409d: mowing machines, harvesters, either self-binding or without binders, binding attachments, reapers, harvesters in combination with threshing machine separators including the motive power incorporated
IMr. McNevin.]
therein, and complete parts of all the foregoing. They are free under all tariffs. The intermediate tariff on goods covered by this item was 7^ per cent and the general tariff twenty-five per cent.
Then take the next item, 409e: spraying and dusting machines and attachments therefor used by fruit growers. These all now come in free.
Then take item 409f: hay loaders, hay tedders, potato planters, potato diggers, fodder or feed cutters, ensilage cutters, grain crushers and grain or hay grinders for farm purposes only, and many other articles. These come in free under all tariffs. This means a reduction of at least 71 per cent.
Then take item 409j: fanning mills; corn husking machines and many other items. These come in free under all tariffs whereas the duty was 71 per cent under the intermediate tariff and twenty-five per cent under the general tariff.
I shall not mention any more items. These examples are sufficient to show that the reduction which has been made in this budget amounts to a reduction on the general line of farm implements running anywhere from 71 to 10 per cent.
Just at the present time when there is such a strong demand for metal products of all kinds for war purposes, placing these implements on the free list may not be of any great immediate benefit to the farmers; but in the years to come, and particularly in the post-war years when there will be a great backlog of demand for farm machinery, and when the farmers will have money with which to buy machinery, I am sure that they will reap substantial benefit from this budget provision for which they have been striving for such a long period of years.
Another matter mentioned by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle was with regard to farmers being placed in a privileged class so far as the payment of income tax was concerned. The suggestion was that they be exempted entirely from, payment of income tax. I am a farmer like the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and personally that would be very fine for me. I do not think any administration could take any action that would do more to promote a back to the land movement than to place all agriculturists in a privileged position so far as payment of income tax is concerned. I do not know of any action that could be taken that W'ould do more to promote larger farming units. Thousands of people who had made their pile would retire _to the country, if agriculturists were exempted from income tax, and would set up a little farm to escape payment of the tax. That proposal might

The Budget-Mr. McNevin
sound well on the election platform, but I am sure that it would not be a sound provision in a budget of the Dominion of Canada.
I wish to make a few remarks upon the magnificent production of agricultural products by the farmers of Canada during this war and to compliment the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) upon the splendid direction and leadership he has given in promoting this remarkable production. I am sure that there have been times when the Canadian people have had misgivings regarding possible food shortages, when they feared that there might be a shortage of food, not only to ship across the seas to feed our armies abroad and the British, but even a shortage of food in Canada to meet the demands of the Canadian people at home. But from year to year we have had an increased production of food products until now everyone in this country seems to be satisfied as to the food situation. I believe that in food production we have established a record that is outstanding in the history of Canadian agriculture.
That brings me to the point of giving some thought to the post-war problems of agriculture. Such thinking and planning must not stand in the way of winning the war as decisively and quickly as possible, because that, of course, represents the major responsibility of the Canadian people.
What will some of these post-war agricultural problems be? The longer the war goes on, the more I am convinced that we are likely to face many of the very same problems faced after the last war, particularly if we fail to support and maintain the price control policy. In my opinion, finding markets for the surplus farm products which the farmer can and will want to produce will be the biggest one. I think the house will agree with me that farmers want to produce all they can. They are never so happy as when they are working at full capacity. Our farmers have surprised Hitler, Tojo, our own people and, in fact, the people of the whole world by showing how much they can produce with a war-time incentive and fair prices. The year 1943 shows the greatest production of food on record in Canada, and 1944, with favourable maturing and harvesting weather conditions, will exceed the record of 1943. This has been accomplished under the handicap of labour shortages and an insufficient supply of machinery and equipment. When we return to peace-time conditions, with the experience we have gained, with the ordinary supply of farm labour and sufficient machinery and equipment, and with fair demand and adequate prices, we can produce, I think hon. members will agree with me, double our pre-war volume of farm products. We have found out in war time how much good, nutritious food the people of this country will consume when they have a sufficiently high income to purchase it in ample supply. But what kind of incomes will our people have in, say 1948? Will our industrial activity be as high as now? Shall we exhibit the same degree of knowledge and determination to conquer unemployment as we have displayed in assisting our allies to conquer the common enemy? The problem must be attacked in that spirit.
But suppose we do have an increase of from fifteen to twenty per cent in our domestic consumption of food-allowing for the normal increase in our population, that is about the best we can hope for-there will still remain a huge surplus to be disposed of in the markets of the world. In facing this great problem let us be honest with ourselves. Even if credits are extended to peoples more unfortunate than we, to buy some of these products, if we are going to sell these surpluses in world markets we must accept the surplus goods of other countries in payment for our exports. This is a hard, indisputable fact. It is not so unpleasant if we remember that we can export our surpluses if we accept the surpluses of other countries-products which they may be able to produce more efficiently than we can- in exchange for our products. Are we ready to advocate lower rather than higher tariffs? Are we ready to agree to fewer trade barriers rather than more? Are we ready to accept and adopt the principle that world trade is a two-way highway, not a single track?
But even if we do succeed in finding an outlet for all our farmers can produce, still we must have a fair price for it before our economic problem is solved. What is satisfactory? Some farm organizations say that parity is a fair price. I prefer to speak in terms of parity of income for farmers rather than parity prices, because parity prices may not result in parity of income. Others say, whatever the law of supply and demand dictates should be the price, even though they know that farmers seem to be the only class subject to this law in its crude, unvarnished form. Too often in the past agriculturists1 have realized that the greater the supply, the less the demand, and consequently the lower the price.
This brings me to the question of bonuses' and fixed prices. Frankly I think these instruments should be retained for a considerable time to come as a protection for
The Budget-Mr. McNevin

both producer and consumer. However, in making this suggestion I am not unmindful of some difficulties which may arise.
First, you can set a price for a commodity but you cannot force the public to purchase it at that price. If the public will not buy as much as the farmers produce, you are in trouble. If the product is perishable, you have not long to wait; if not, it can be stored but the evil day is only delayed.
Then in the matter of prices, what we in Canada think is a fair price may be a high price to some other countries. In fact, if world prices were as high as ours, world production would probably be much higher, causing a curtailment of demand for our surpluses.
Let us also review past experiences with bonused or subsidized products which were exported. The experiences were not too happy. It can drive down world prices still farther, because in a buyers' market everyone tries to meet the low price and the price frequently falls. If our price is substantially higher than the world price it is an inducement for other countries to sell in our markets. The suggestion that tariff or trade barriers will set things right is not a sound one. As a solution, I suggest that these problems are worldwide and must be attacked from that point ;of view. Nations cannot longer live unto themselves alone. In Canada measures have been taken during war time which should be very helpful in the post-war period.
First and foremost of these is the price control policy so ably devised and administered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). This policy has won the admiration of financial leaders and critics throughout the world. It should be more appreciated and better understood by the Canadian people. So far it has beaten inflation. Given support to carry this policy through, we have overcome post-war's most formidable enemy.
We must approach the problems of reconstruction determined that unemployment must be licked. I think we have learned that the greatest single example of waste in the world is permitting human hands to be idle when food and goods which people need could be produced. We surely can agree that increasing consumption to support prices is cheaper and more effective than restricting production to support prices. This should go for industry, labour and agriculture. The bill which will soon be before the house to provide for family allowances is an example of a move to increase consumption and support production in the manner I have just indicated. We have learned much out of the experience of the
(Mr. McNevin.]
past, and if we intelligently apply that knowledge we should go forward with courage and confidence. We have found the money to do our share in winning the war; we must do likewise to win the peace. In the broader field of world affairs, particularly as applied to the war, Churchill, Chiang Kai-shek, Stalin, Roosevelt and Mackenzie King have found a common foundation upon which to unite their efforts to win this, the most titanic war in history. I am not going to suggest what should be done in other countries, but I would suggest, as far as the Canadian people are concerned, that we should maintain at the helm of our ship of state the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King to meet with these world leaders and to find a common foundation upon which they can unite to win the peace as they have united to win the war.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The budget this year is indicative of a tremendous gamble. The underlying principles of the entire speech are based on the possibility of an early collapse of Germany. There may be some justification in taking this gamble, and gamble it is, for this is the only excuse for the inflationary measures proposed by the government's policy. The government has entirely reversed its previous policy, and instead of endeavouring to provide a high level of employment, it has adopted the specious and entirely unacceptable policy of paternalism. Paternalism never has been and never will be a substitute for independence through individual effort. If the gamble taken is successful and the shell of fortress Europe, once broken, detonates an internal collapse, then the government will be immediately faced with the problem of rehabilitating our armed forces; for once the now overwhelming weight of allied power is concentrated against the ferine and barbaric island of Japan, her utter destruction will not take long to accomplish. Without in any way minimizing the task ahead, I wish at this time to discuss one of the major problems of the reconstruction period and one which I believe will do more than any other to preserve our present bountiful economy on a high level of employment.
I wish to speak of the mining industry and in particular of the question of mining taxation. As is generally known, we have been blessed with a larger potential area for mining development than any other country in the world. Climatically, the Canadian shield may be considered to be rigorous, but when compared with the extreme temperature of Siberia, reaching as low as ninety degrees below zero, and the other extreme of Africa, India, and South America, where the

The Budget-Mr. Adamson
rock temperatures underground may reach as high as 120 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit, it will be seen that we are indeed very fortunate. In the period of depression Canadian mines, particularly the precious metal mines, provided one of the greatest sources of permanent employment. It is said by the Wallace committee that 107,000 people were directly employed by the industry, giving employment indirectly to 1,200,000 or over one-tenth of our total population. At no time during the depression did our relief roll approach this figure, and I suggest to the house that had our mining industry been fifty per cent larger than it was, there would have been virtually no men on relief in this dominion during those years.
The mining industry is unlike all other industries. To be continuous it must be constantly replenishing itself. New mines must be found; the ground must be prepared; capital, particularly risk capital, must be encouraged and the prospector must at all times find a ready market for his services; for he holds the key which will unlock the golden treasury. Our present taxation policy has brought about the very opposite of this, until to-day we find our mining industry in the following shocking condition. Of Canada's 1942 metal production, fifty-six per cent was derived from mineral areas discovered prior to 1910, over a third of a century ago; twenty-eight per cent was derived from the mineral areas discovered between 1910 and 1920; that is, eighty-four per cent from areas discovered over a quarter of a century ago; eleven per cent was derived from mineral areas discovered between 1920 and 1930, and only five per cent came from mineral areas discovered since 1930. This is one of the most serious indictments against the federal government.
Mining, Mr. Speaker, is essentially a risk business. When success is found the rewards are great, but the ratio of success to failure will, I think, surprise hon. members of this house. It is a fact that less than one per cent of the companies incorporated for the purpose of metal mine development during the thirty-five year period from 1907 to 1941 inclusive could be classified as having attained economic success. The average actual taxpaying or profitable productive life of a precious metals mine in the central provinces is indicated to be less than eight years. Furthermore, during the thirty-five year period from 1907 to 1941 inclusive only one-third of the productive metal mines in Ontario had reached the stage of taxable profits recorded earnings, which enabled them to return invested capital to their shareholders. It therefore follows that the remaining two-thirds of these mines were actually taxed on capital.
As an example of the amount of capital required to develop a mine, it is authoritatively stated that the Hudson Bay Mining company at Flin Flon, Manitoba, required an expenditure of $30 million before any return was made to the shareholders. The Noranda mine-I think the minister will support me in this because he has made this very statement himself-required $25 million to enable it to produce and refine the metals of copper and gold. Furthermore, the average straight gold mines required from $2 million to $5 million to bring them into profitable production and to begin to return capital invested. These are very large sums and they must be considered as being risk capital.
This is one of the most valuable of all types of capital because it directly develops a primary industry of the nation. It is easily discouraged, and because of the hazardous natural and physical obstacles which it has to surmount, the addition of tax burdens will rapidly kill it at its source.
One of the fundamental errors made by the government is the method of assessing mine profits. In this connection I should like to quote from the brief on mining taxation by the Ontario and Quebec governments, submitted jointly by the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy in February of this year. I quote two paragraphs:
(a)	Taxing authorities do not appreciate sufficiently the fundamental difference betw'een mining and other industries.
(b)	Insufficient provision is made in the allowance for depletion to ensure return of invested capital. Anyone investing in mines recognizes that he has no profit until his capital is returned. The government should likewise recognize this fact. Taxes on real profits can begin only after provision has been made for the return of invested capital.
Before 1934, depletion allowance for gold mines was fifty per cent of the net earnings on both mine profits and dividends. Base metal mines were allowed depletion of twenty-five per cent. In 1934, depletion allowance for all mines was set at 334- per cent and on dividends paid to Canadians was reduced to a minimum rate of twenty per cent. These rates are still in effect, and I should like to quote again from the brief on taxation:
This unexplainable reduction in depletion allowance has been one of the most serious factors contributing to the decline in prospecting and new mine development. The federal tax is applicable to income and not to capital return. The present 33J per cent depletion allowance is presumed to be the proportion of annual earnings earmarked for this return; but when actual distribution of this capital is made in the form of dividends the federal taxing authorities rule that only twenty per cent of each capital shall be tax free. Surely this is at least illogical. It should be noted that the
The Budget-Mr. Adamson

increased revenue derived by the government through this reduction in depletion allowance was not for war purposes. The change became effective five years prior to the outbreak of the present war.
Analysis of the application of the present depletion allowance of 33J per cent of company earnings, and twenty per cent for dividend, clearly demonstrates that, while the intention may have been to make provision for 33J per cent of earnings as tax-free capital return, the actual return to the shareholders falls far short of that proportion.

It is generally agreed that a gold mining stock should pay ten per cent or sell at ten times the dividend paid. If this be true, let us suppose a mining company pays SI a year in dividends, and that its stock sells for ten times $1 or $10.
Under the allowances of 33J per cent and 20 per cent it will take a shareholder 1009i4-6, or nearly seventy years to get his capital back free of tax.
Under the proposed fifty per cent to company and shareholder alike, it would take the same company 100%o, or twenty-five years to do the same thing.

In the tax brief that I have quoted previously, it is shown that, taking all gold mining companies that have paid the so-called profits tax in Ontario, the average taxpaying life of such companies is about eight years.
The experience of our mining history has shown that to be true. Under such circumstances, asking that the period be not over twenty-five years, when the average chance is limited to eight years, cannot surely be considered as unreasonable. By the same token, seventy years must be unreasonable.

If we take the profits of a straight gold mine we find this picture. The McIntyre Porcupine operation, which is a successful operation in every way, paid the following taxes during the last fiscal year. The total taxes were $1,214,437, representing an amount of $1,029 for every man employed, or $6.42 for every ounce of gold recovered, or $1.52 for every share of stock outstanding. In addition there are the municipal taxes and the taxes paid by individual shareholders. The over-all picture in Ontario from 1915 to 1941 is as follows: Dominion taxes increased from $130,000 to $11,324,000. The total tax per ton of ore milled increased from 24 cents to $1.15. The cost per ounce of gold increased from 56 cents to $4.51. The total tax on operations of the Ontario gold mining indus-

The Budget-Mr. Adamson
try, plus estimated dominion income tax on all dividends, increased from 9-4 per cent in 1917 to 48-5 per cent in 1941; or, expressed in another way, it increased to 48J cents for every dollar of dividends, or 52-2 per cent on established gold mines not subject to section 89 of the income tax act. It is estimated that the taxation at present is approximately 60 per cent of the total returns made to the shareholders in Ontario mines. This compares with 18-5 per cent in 1928 which unfortunately was the last year of intensive mining development.
The situation in Quebec is possibly more serious because of the generally lower grade mines in that province. No province in this dominion has a deeper interest in this question of low grade ores than Quebec. Of that province's twenty-four gold producing mines no less than thirteen have a grade of S5 a ton or less. These thirteen produce sixty per cent of Quebec's gold. To-day $5 a ton is considered pretty close to the line; with numerous mines in Canada the costs are well above this figure. It is only by dint of the fact that Quebec's ore bodies are large and lend themselves to large scale mining, and because of good management and the helpful interest which the province of Quebec takes in its mines, that these low grade propositions are able to run at all. The people of Quebec are closely watching this government to see whether it follows a policy which encourages mining endeavour, or pursues 'a policy of discouragement. I say this because the people of Quebec have utilized the disclosures of gold and other mining resources in their northwestern areas as the foundation of a very important plan of agricultural settlement. The frontier farms upon which numerous people work skilfully and prosperously lose all the market outlets for their labour when the gold mines fail. Hence the very deep concern when the operation of any Quebec gold mine appears to be endangered by shortage of labour. Fortunately for Quebec, no important Quebec gold mine has had to close down by reason of labour shortage, although in the rest of Canada many gold mines have had to quit completely and leave their communities in a very difficult state, in some places on the edge of bankruptcy. I mention Quebec because, as every one in the mining business knows, its mines, while very important, are often on the low grade side. Taxation of a character which cripples the use of low grade ores and which checks the enterprise of mine-makers is of very special interest to the province of Quebec.
Of the forty pure gold mines operating in Ontario-those that rely solely upon goldonly five have a grade of $5 a ton or less. I do not know whether this means that Ontario is more blessed with higher grade gold mines than the other provinces of Canada. Probably it means that conditions in Ontario have not been such as to encourage the development of low grade propositions. Undoubtedly Ontario would have more such mines if the taxation set-up was more favourable to people taking chances on mines in the low grade category.
In order to make my point clear as to the value of low grade ore-

speechtext:
I am coming to that, if the minister will contain himself. If he had listened to the beginning of my speech his question would have been answered. Perhaps he will read it to-morrow in Hansard.
In order to make my point clear about the value of low grade ore some brief discussion of the way the ore bearing solutions were injected might overcome some misconception which I believe to be common. This is a dangerous subject to tackle, because it is difficult to generalize and the science of geology is vast and complicated. However, with your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, let the house imagine a drum of boiling white paraffin. Now into the bottom of this drum is injected, under great pressure, a number of cupfuls of boiling red paraffin. The drum is then allowed to cool. When the wax has solidified, if we cut into it we shall possibly find the red paraffin in a pillar-shaped or lenticular-shaped mass, depending on the method of injection. However, we will find it not in one even mass but mixed with the white paraffin, and while the centre of the mass may still be quite red in colour it will soon become pink; then only slightly coloured as we proceed from the centre of the mass until there is no trace of colour whatsoever.
This is something of the same way the ore bearing solutions were absorbed into the native pre-Cambrian rock of the Canadian shield. The solutions rich in the centre soon were dissolved in the country rock into which they were forced by volcanic action. Of course it was not as simple as this; many different volcanic eruptions took place and great earthquakes subsequently caused ground movement, breaking up the original ore mass and moving parts of it great distances from the main body. However, the principle of the ore bearing solutions flowing into, and being absorbed and diluted by the country rock,
The Budget-Mr. Adamson

just as the red paraffin flowed into the white, holds good. So that as we get variation in colour of the paraffin we get the variation in value of the resultant mass of rock which we now find in situ. The problem of the miner is to get every pound of the rich solution just as it would be to get every cupful of the red paraffin vrax, assuming it to have great value. The miner would fail to do this if he merely took out the rich centre section of the ore body, just as he would fail if he only took the bright red paraffin which had not become diluted by the white.
This rather fanciful allegory has considerable importance and is one of the fundamental conditions of mining which is not understood by the tax gatherer; for just as the greater quantity of the red paraffin wdll be found in dilute solution with the white, so is the vast majority of the original metal bearing deposit in dilute solution in the native rock. Estimates vary, but for every ton of $10 ore in place in the majority of our precious metal mines, there will be many tons of $5 ore and many, many more tons of $4 and $3 ore.
An empirical theory of ore valuations in a simple arithmetical progression has been suggested, and while this does not of course work exactly in any one mine, or cannot be applied to all mines, it approximates conditions in several of our major gold producers. The theory is that for every ton of $10 ore there are two tons of $9 ore, four tons of $8 ore and sixteen tons of $7 ore and so on. Carrying the progression down to $3 we get the following results:
