It will be seen that an ore body of this kind -always assuming that we take out all the rock to $3, which is approximately the minimum that any mine to-day can take out- will contain 255 tons of ore each containing more than $3 worth of metal and it will have a total value of $912. The average value per ton of such a body will be only $3.58. If we discard all rock containing $5 or less in metal, the value of the remainder will be $5.90 per ton. Thus, as our costs of mining increase from $3 to $5, we find that we lose $640 or 70 per cent of the dollar value of the whole ore body. It will be seen, therefore, how tremendously destructive taxation is which increases the cost of ore milled, and when we

see that at Noranda the total tax per ton of ore hoisted has increased from sixty cents in 1932 to $2.29 in 1941, some idea of this tremendous destruction of ore may be gathered.
An ore body which has once been mined and has had the rich centre core removed, can never be worked again, because the low grade remaining in the side walls will not pay for extraction. This is of fundamental importance. The process is known as high-grading the mine and it is as harmful to the people of Canada as is high-grading the mine by individuals, because it definitely steals from the people of the country one of their assets. It is tragic to think that the government of the people tolerates this criminal practice.
Lest anybody think our supplies of nickel are inexhaustible I should like to quote from the report of its president, Mr. E. C. Stanley. This is what he said:
Deliveries of nickel in all forms derived from our own mine production amounted in 1943 to
265.000.	009 pounds, representing an increase of
55.000.	000 pounds over 1939. In order to provide this enlarged supply, the tonnage of our ore mined was forced from 7,273,000 tons in 1939 to 12,105,000 tons in 1943.
This means that Canada's largest mining organization has suffered a very considerable decline in the grade of its ore. The recovered content in 1939 was thirty pounds per ton. By 1943 it had dropped to twenty-two pounds per ton. The margin is getting thin. It was necessary to increase the tonnage created by sixty-five per cent to gain a production of nickel only twenty-five per cent greater. The high grade deposits of the Sudbury district are fading. This is the greatest nickel camp in the world and the reason for Canada producing eighty-five per cent of the world's nickel. The world has many low grade nickel ore deposits;-they are to be found in numerous countries. If the high grade nickel ores of Canada are ever exhausted, then all our boasted supremacy in nickel fades away.
It is a serious situation for Canada, or could be if cognizance is not taken of it. During the war we have encouraged our nickel mines to produce to the utmost of their ability, and their achievements in that line demand the warmest of praise. But they have paid a heavy cost in the exhaustion of their better ores. It is our good fortune that these companies still have 250,000,000 tons of ore in reserve, or about twenty years normal supply, and though the average grade is lower we can hope that the skill of our nickel miners will put this lower grade to good account. But they will be handicapped, if not badly crippled, unless we ease the burden of taxation.

The Budget-Mr. Adamson
Some 15,000 or 16,000 men in Canada are engaged in the mining and refining of nickel, and we owe consideration to them, and the 150,000 persons who are supported one way and another by the nickel industry, as well as consideration to Canada's prestige as the world's chief producer of nickel.
I should like to say something about copper. We must think in terms of big tonnage for the future of our copper production. On the Arctic coasts of Canada there are believed to be large masses of low grade copper ore, and it is probably true that elsewhere in Canada other large deposits of low grade copper ore exist. It may well be that we shall be forced to consider the mining of these, and eventually we shall see in this dominion, operations as large as Kennecott's famous Utah Copper Mine where last year 59J million tons of ore were mined and forty-nine million tons of earth were stripped. Operations of this order, and indeed any large-tonnage proposition, require great sums of capital. It is impossible to attract such huge investment on a small margin of profit, unless the investors know that taxation will not rob them of a chance to get their money back, plus a return commensurate with the risks.
The seriousness of the situation is well recognized by the Wallace committee in a report to- this house. I shall quote three paragraphs from that report as follows:
1.	Intensified search for and discovery of new sources of supply is indispensable if the Canadian mineral industry is to survive.
2.	Ores of metals vary greatly in the percentage of metal contained and in the percentage recovered. The lower the cost of recovery the greater will be tile tonnage of ore available for treatment. Taxation charged as a cost against alining reduces the amount of metal that can profitably be recovered from a given mine. The higher the tax, the greater the loss of metal that might otherwise have been recovered.
There is a wide field for extending employment provided new sources of mineral wealth are found and new methods of utilizing those rocks and minerals, which occur in great abundance, are developed.
The essential requirements are intensive stimulation of prospecting, the provision of maps, topographical and geological, the provision of transportation facilities (roads, et cetera) into mining areas, a minimum of restrictive measures so that the prospector may continue to. be stimulated by the possibility of a find that will compensate him for years of disappointment.
3.	That adjustments be made in respect to taxation that would stimulate prospecting and mine development and mineral recovery.
And finally, I recommend to this house the careful study of clause 20, which contains this significant sentence: "An expanding mining industry will be of particular national importance and should be carefully studied." The
whole report of the Wallace committee deserves the most careful attention and, I believe, represents one of the best blueprints for the future that has yet been produced.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) went to great lengths in his statement to this house to compare our taxation with that of Australia. He should have been more thorough, for there are many, many instances where Australian taxation is far more generous than ours; generous let me say from a realistic point of view, because Australia, during a wave of extreme socialistic government, all but destroyed her mining industry, and the present administration has had to enact special encouragement classes of her income tax act in order to save the industry from extinction. I may say that if the present government persists in its policies the mining industry in Canada will also face extinction. I will quote the Australian act. Section 23, in the first line, reads as follows:-
The following income shall be exempt from income tax.
And paragraph (m) reads as follows:
(m) income derived prior to the first day of July, one thousand nine hundred and forty-seven, directly and in the first place from primary production, mining or fisheries in the Northern Territory of Australia by a resident of that territory.
There are three clauses dealing with exemption which I think are of great interest. I have already quoted paragraph (m), and now I will quote paragraph (o):
(o) the income derived by a person from the working of a mining property in Australia or in the territory of New Guinea principally for the purpose of obtaining gold, or gold and copper, provided that in this case the value of the output of gold is not less than forty per centum of the total value of the output of the mine.
Paragraph (p) provides that income derived by a bona fide prospector shall be exempt from income tax, and bona fide prospector is defined, and is a very broad definition.
If we applied paragraph (m) to Canada it would mean that all the present development in the Northwest Territories, including the Yellowknife field, would be exempt from taxation. I suggest to the house that if we did this in the immediate post-war years there would be a gold rush, the like of which has not been seen in history.
In connection with the Northwest Territories and the much publicized Yellowknife discoveries, it should be pointed out that this is not a new thing. For many years past, prospectors have been in this country and there have been a number of actually producing mines, one the Conn mine, a subsidiary of Consolidated Smelters, and another the Negus
The Budget-Mr. Adamson

mine, which has actually reached the dividend paying state, having returned its shareholders five cents a share during 1943.

speechtext:
May I conclude this paragraph, Mr. Speaker? I should like to go on record as supporting the contention of the Ontario and Quebec governments that th$ depletion allowance of fifty per cent on the net earnings of all metal mines be allowed and that this be extended to dividends as declared.
Secondly, that taxes paid to municipalities and provincial authorities be allowed as a deduction.
Thirdly, that all exploration expenditures made outside the property of the mine be allowed as a deduction from earnings.
If we went as far as Australia we would exempt from taxation both corporation, income and excess profit taxes on all metal mines. I believe if we did this the treasury of the dominion government and the rate of employment would both benefit. However, certain precautions would have to be taken. We would have to see that every profitable mining operation did its fair share of exploration and prospecting; secondly, we would have to see that once a percentage of capital had been returned to the company, the net earnings or a considerable proportion of them would be paid to the individual shareholders. We must safeguard our country from operators who would build up large surpluses and then take them out of Canada.
I realize that in this life and death struggle any taxation, no matter how unsound, or how discriminatory, will be paid and paid gladly; but when I see the Minister of Finance bringing down clauses which are obviously peacetime clauses, I feel that some statement of policy should be made with regard to the future of the mining industry, upon which more than all others the future of Canada depends.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) on June 26 introduced into this house his sixth wartime budget of world war two. It is a budget of very large proportions calling for an expenditure of almost six billion dollars. This in itself is a huge amount of money for a population of eleven million people to contemplate. It is a budget that arrests our attention when we realize that it is about eleven times our ordinary peace-time expenditure. However, I am sure that the people of this country recognize the importance of an expenditure of this kind and are prepared to

shoulder the load and carry the taxation responsibility that goes with the prosecution of an all-out war.
It was, of course, gratifying for the minister to be able to say that approximately one-half of the revenue required for the huge expenditure last year had been raised through the general revenues and that the remainder had been largely borrowed from our own people through the sale of victory bonds and war savings certificates, and the minister hopes that the same creditable record will be achieved in the year to come. Here is one place where I think we as members of parliament can lend to the minister and to the government and to the country generally a degree of cooperation, regardless of the political differences that may exist between us. We have called upon the people of this country to come forward and lend their money and to pay taxes. I think we owe to the national war finance committee and to the thousands of volunteers who have acted with them in putting across our various victory loan campaigns a debt of gratitude which we shall be a long time in repaying. I feel that we owe to these workers a deep debt of gratitude and should lend them every assistance possible when the opportunity comes to promote another victory loan.
While taxation is high and while some of the regulations that we have during war time may be irritating, nevertheless they are a small amount of insurance for what Canada has been able to do. We are here a nation that has been at war; yet we have never had a city bombed nor has a foreign soldier set foot upon our soil, so that I think it is small insurance for us to pay when the chief obligations that are required of us are to pay out a little money to meet the taxation requirements of the country.
We have at the same time enjoyed a degree of prosperity which we have never enjoyed before in the history of this dominion, nor has that prosperity ever before been as equitably distributed as it is at the present time. The contribution, therefore, that we are called upon as civiliains to pay in this war in the way of taxation and in the way of putting up with regulations and little inconveniences is small compared with the hardships which the men on the actual fighting fronts have to bear at this time.
While the minister has seen fit to discontinue the refundable portion of the income tax, I must say that I felt right along that this feature of our taxation had much to commend it. It provided a means for creating a savings, a nest-egg for the future; and when it is realized that the refundable portion of the-

The Budget-Mr. Weir
income tax oould be offset by the payment of insurance premiums and the payment of principal on farm mortgages and on mortgages on homes, I cannot see that the burden was so very great for the vast majority of people, particularly those who are in a position to make such payments. For those who are not in that position, the refundable savings feature provided a means whereby they could accumulate a sum for the period when the war is over. After all, the majority of the people whom the minister hopes to benefit most in this regard, those in the low income tax brackets, will only secure, I imagine, the advantage of perhaps two or three dollars a week, which may easily be expended for non-essentials, instead of being set aside as a savings for the post-war period.
As was to be expected, the other political groups in this house have offered counterproposals. In other words, they would do things differently from the way the minister proposes. They believe that their proposals will appeal more strongly to the people at this particular time.
While the minister has done away with the refundable portion of the income tax, our Progressive Conservative friends opposite would raise the income tax exemption to S800 a year for single persons and $1,600 for married people, and at the same time create a fund equal to the contribution that we make to UNRRA as an amount of money available for the post-war period. Our Cooperative Commonwealth Federation friends would go one better and raise the exemption respectively to $1,000 and to fifteen or sixteen hundred dollars, and also provide $5,000 million for a two-year period after the war. It is easy for them to bring forward such proposals at this time; indeed it is their privilege that they should do so. On the other hand, the Minister of Finance is in a responsible position and must carry into effect anything that he proposes to the house. The opposition groups are able to offer proposals which they do not hope to implement, certainly at the present time; but he is obliged to face up to his proposals now and lay his plans for the whole government programme. These people present their proposals as a different method of doing things. I believe that the objective of all of us is the same. We want to prosecute this war to the end as effectively as possible. The opposition group propose to do so by a different method.
This reminds me of a traveller who was sent out from his head office to a country town. Arriving there in the early hours of the morning, he found that the railway station was a
mile or two from the business and hotel section. He looked around and could find neither street-car nor taxicab to carry him to the hotel. Finally he spoke to the station agent, who mentioned that probably the mail carrier would be down and he might get a ride to the city with him later on. At last the mail carrier arrived and the traveller secured a ride with him. He began to complain bitterly of the railway station being two or three miles away from the business section of the town, when it should have been put in the middle of the town, near the hotels, as a convenience to the travelling public. The old gentleman who drove the mails, and who had been in the town for some time, finally said, "Young man, you may be right in what you say, but there are a lot of people around here who think it is much better to have the station down beside the railway track." He had a practical approach to the problem at hand, which is the approach the Minister of Finance is up against at the present time.
May I say to the minister that, while he has affected in a direct way more people than any other minister of this government, he still holds their confidence and admiration. There is no minister who has gone into the people's pockets and collected taxes, made regulations and fixed wages and price ceilings- things of that kind-to the same extent as the Minister of Finance has done; yet he enjoys the admiration of the Canadian people for what he has achieved. Moreover, he has had the satisfaction of receiving commendation from people outside our country who have watched with keen interest the success he has made of the financing of this country during this period of war. More than that, many of the policies which were established by this government during the early stages of the war have been copied in large measure by other countries.
May I here read a little tribute to him which was carried in Saturday Night a few days ago;
Common Sense
Mr. 1 Lsley's conduct as Minister of Finance has been characterized by a degree of common sense so uncommon as to be astounding. It is pure common sense to abandon the compulsory saving device, which in principle has every argument in its favour except that it works badly. It is pure common sense to extend the tax allowance to illegitimate children and to relatives-in-law. It is pure common sense not to stick on any more taxes at this moment. It is excellent common sense to make the refundable portion of the excess profits tax a valid collateral for borrowing. We still believe that common sense will, some day, when he gets around to it, lead him to distinguish between capital payments and the interest or profit element in annuities. Meanwhile we can assure
The Budget-Mr. Weir

that the country loves him for his common sense almost as much as for his courage and his honesty.
There are three features of the government's war-time policy which to me have been fundamental from the beginning, and are now, and will be more so in the post-war period. It is unfortunate that they have not been more loudly proclaimed to the people of this country so that they may be better understood. Our price control policy has held prices stable. The result has been that it has maintained in this country a price structure which will be of inestimable value when the war is over. Some time ago I met some friends who had been to the United States, and who told me some of the experiences they had in visiting a home in that country. They pointed out that people over there were loud in their praise of Canadian policies particularly with respect to price control and its enforcement. The lady of the house remarked that since the beginning of the war the cost of running her house had risen from $20 a week to $35 a week and she did not know where the money had gone. Her little boy, eight years old, came in with a haircut which cost $1. That is some indication of what can happen, and some evidence of the advantage which we have under our price control system.
The other matter to which I wish to refer is the policy of borrowing from ourselves. This has had a far-reaching and fundamental effect. It has created a sense of thrift in the accumulation of savings and the paying off of debt. I believe the country will be gratified to know from the statement of the Minister of Finance that our debt, so far as the financing of this war is concerned, is owned to the extent of ninety-five per cent by ourselves.
I come to the income tax and excess profits system. Here, to me, is a great over-all experiment in the application of state socialism. It is applied on the basis of ability to pay, upon a graduated basis whereby those who have shall pay most. Our socialist friends, so far as I have heard or observed their various proposals, have never proposed anything as sweeping and far-reaching of a socialistic nature as our income tax system. It is a great social experiment which is working well and doing a job of equalizing opportunity and incomes. It is a social experiment with far-reaching effect. I often wonder why our hon. friends on the other side of the house cannot once in a while give us some little credit for the steps which have been taken in this particular regard.
There were three features of the budget proposals which I was particularly glad to see. It is a source of satisfaction to me that

the foreign exchange control tax and the tariff have been lifted from farm implements. The provision will include all classes of farm implements, from dairy utensils and the smallest type of implements right up to power machinery. My feeling has always been that there was little if any justification for the foreign exchange control tax ever to have been applied to tractors and power equipment of that kind. We do not manufacture tractors in this country, so that I think we were imposing a burden of cost on our farmers which w'as unnecessary. May I pause, however, to point out one thing which to me does not work out with that degree of equity and fairness which I think matters of this kind should. When the foreign exchange control tax was applied, the implement companies and others naturally added the amount of that tax to their inventory. Some of them even showed it as- an added tax. Now it is presumed, and I think they would admit it immediately, that once *that tax is removed they will be expected to reduce their prices on imported implements to an extent equal to the amount of the tax. But the point I would call to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) is that the same people had large inventories when this tax was applied and to-day they have little or no equipment in their warehouses, so that to me there was a class of people there who were called upon to pay a tax which they were not justified in paying.
With respect to the application of the income tax on farmers, I am glad to note the improvement that has been suggested. However, I do not think it goes far enough, and I believe our taxation authorities would be well advised to give a good deal more study to the application of the income tax so far as the farm business of the country is concerned. We hear a good deal of complaint and some good-natured gibes at the type of income tax forms which farmers are obliged to fill out. That is not the point. When we have farmers in nine different provinces, from one end of the country to the other, it is recognized that an income tax form must be all-embracing in order to provide for the various types of farming operations that are carried on. My contention has always been and still is that the income tax, so far as our farmers are concerned, should be applied on an average of a five-year basis. At the present time some $60 million is being paid out on participation certificates on wheat which was marketed in the years 1940, 1941 and 1942. If that money becomes taxable in the current yrear, then I think it is unfair, and I hope the minister will see to it that

The Budget-Mr. Weir
at least that money can be applied on the income tax year for which it was earned or in which the crop was marketed.
The other matter I should like to urge continued consideration of is that which applies to a farmer who sells out or liquidates his chattels. It seems to me to be grossly unfair, where a man has accumulated a certain amount of live stock and other products over a period of years, that when he is obliged to sell out for one reason or another, that is taken as income. If the minister has evolved regulations which will solve this very important problem I hope he will take an opportunity of making an announcement with regard to it.
Another matter regarding which I wish to make an observation or two is that of the taxation of cooperatives. I am not going to refer to this because I understand it is improper to do so, except to say that I think it is unfortunate and regrettable that this matter has not been settled. We have hundreds of these cooperative organizations small in size serving the people of western Canada, and to have them in a state of uncertainty with regard to their taxation status is most unfortunate. It is something that should be remedied at as early a date as possible.
May I for a moment say a word or two about the post-war period. One would think, listening to the observations of hon. gentlemen in various parts of the house, that nothing had been done by this government or by anyone else looking toward the post-war period. As illustrative of that point of view, I refer again to the one group proposing to spend some $75 or $80 million immediately on the close of the war, and the other, $5 billion over a two-year period. I submit that the whole programme of this government has been designed from the beginning to meet both the war period and the post-war period as well. The wide distribution of victory bonds and war savings certificates will be one of the most important instruments we have in meeting the post-war period. Millions of Canadians will have their own resources to assist them in tiding over from the period of war into the period of peace. There is a backlog of work to be done and supplies to be provided which will, in my judgment, tax the resources of the people of this country for a considerable period. It is the period later than that immediate postwar period that I fear more.
In my approach particularly to the post-war period, may I say that if I am anything at all I hope I am a ruralist. While I appreciate your big cities and what they can contribute to the betterment of mankind, nevertheless I do not think they would last very long or be
able to maintain their splendid services, the high educational facilities and other things of that kind, if it were not for the production received from the primary producers and other rural people. Rural Canada needs repairs and needs them badly. It needs new buildings; it needs actually trainloads of paint and of lumber; it needs literally thousands of carpenters. If given an opportunity, I believe it will provide a degree of employment equal to any other branch of industry in this country. Rural Canada in my judgment needs hydro electric power, particularly lighting facilities. Compared with other countries in this regard we are very much behind. I have checked up some figures and I repeat them for the benefit of the house. Hydro electric service is supplied in Sweden to seventy-five per cent of the farms; in Denmark, eighty-five per cent; in Holland, ninety-eight per cent; in France, ninety per cent; in New Zealand, seventy-five per cent; in the United States, forty-two per cent; and in Ontario, which so far as our country is concerned has much the largest amount of hydro, it is only forty per cent, while in Manitoba it is down to two per cent.
The development of hydro and its extension throughout Manitoba will be, I think, one of the large over-all post-war projects in that province. It in turn will provide a great deal of employment both in the establishment of the lines and in the production of equipment that is necessary to go with the extension of a large development of hydro facilities. This will require capital at a low rate of interest. If that capital can be secured for extension purposes at a low rate of interest, those acquiring it can make their capital investment self-liquidating through their earnings from rentals on the Winnipeg river. This to me would be an overall plan for post-war development of a self-liquidating nature. At the present time meetings are being held all over the province laying out plans, interesting local bodies, municipalities and boards of trade with a view to providing for the best possible utilization and expansion of hydro facilities. Nothing will do more to remove the drudgery and brighten up farm life than will paint and hydro electric power. Hand in hand with a development of that kind I would hope to see in our western provinces a further industrial development, particularly in the processing of agricultural products of a perishable or semi-perishable nature.
I have been through certain parts of this fine province of Ontario and have seen some of the developments that have gone on there with respect to cold storage facilities, quick-freeze plants, and things of that kind. May I say that so far as. Manitoba is concerned it is capable of producing practically any type of farm product that is produced in Ontario and
The Budget-Mr. Weir

in most of the other parts of eastern Canada, with the possible exception of special lines on a commercial scale. Nearly all small fruits and vegetables can be produced in that province. Therefore, anything that we can do toward making them more available for general use is something that I am sure should be undertaken. The farm people in the west are entitled to encouragement along this line and I hope that steps will be taken to that end.
As I said earlier, I believe that it will provide a great deal of employment. Speaking again as a ruralist, I should like to see as a post-war over-all development something in the way of assistance toward the development of community life. It might be the establishment of community halls or recreational centres and things of that kind, whereby people could take advantage of their local talents and develop them into more useful purposes, with a view to taking part on any occasion when they may be called on. A policy of that kind could do much toward *developing a community spirit and a unity of purpose, particularly in some of our more or less non-English speaking districts. There we could bring those people together and do much toward developing in them a Canadianism. After all, they have much to contribute to our everyday life, and anything that we can *do to encourage them is to our advantage.
I wanted to make a reference to housing. I do not come from an industrial constituency and therefore I have not quite the same appreciation of this matter as members from large cities have; but I say to you, Mr. Speaker, without hesitation, that the need for housing is very great in large areas of rural western Canada. The people who appear to be most in need at the present time are those who live in the smaller towns. Our approved lending institutions have not given them the same attention as they have to larger areas. I hope that the smaller towns will be kept in mind in any programme that may be worked out in the new proposals which are to be introduced.
I hope that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) can be assisted in further expanding and developing the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. Water conservation and development and reclamation schemes are all part and parcel of a post-war programme. I wonder if people realize just what prairie farm rehabilitation has meant to the production of live stock, so badly needed during this particular war period. There were put down in western Canada some eighteen thousand dugouts to supply water for farmers to produce live stock who in a large measure were previously unable to do so. Therefore I hope
 '
that steps will be taken to see that the minister has an opportunity to develop further the prairie farm rehabilitation! programme.
I had intended to refer to some of the other matters that the government is undertaking looking toward the post-war period. But as my time has nearly expired I shall refer to them only briefly. Some people would attempt to lead the country to believe that the government has done nothing toward post-war planning. Earlier I made reference to what I thought was part and parcel of the government's programme with respect to the war and the post-war period. The plans made at the beginning had in mind not only the war period, but also the post-war period as well. Since that time the government has instituted several far-reaching inquiries and investigations, and called in the most capable people who could be gathered around it to give advice. I recall that in 1941 a committee of reconstruction was set up under Doctor Cyril James of McGill university to study post-war problems and make recommendations to the government. That committee has submitted a report, and those hon. members who have taken occassion to read it must have recognized that it is a comprehensive report. Later a committee was appointed on economic policy under the chairmanship of the deputy minister of finance. Then a committee of this House of Commons has been studying reconstruction and rehabilitation matters for the past few years. People and officials from all walks of life have appeared before this committee. In fact, reading the evidence and recognizing the witnesses who have appeared one finds it hard to conceive of any branch of the post-war problem that has not been given attention by this committee. It is still carrying on its activities. Then we have the committee on social security which has been carrying on for two years.
I had intended to speak particularly on some of the matters outside Canada and in which Canada is playing a leading part. I refer to international conferences looking toward the post-war period, looking to the time when the war will be over and when-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, thank you. My time is just about up. When plans can be made for the period of peace, HNRRA, in which Canada plays an important part, is one of those. The conference on food and nutrition, attended by forty different nations is a study of post-war nutritional matters. Then there were certain proposals put forward by the governments of the United States and Great Britain with respect to post-war monetary

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy
policy, particularly the establishment of a unified system of exchange. Here again Canada submitted a proposal which met with a very large measure of approval. At the present time, I am informed, this matter is being dealt with at a conference of representatives of forty-seven of the united nations, who are. seeking an agreement in regard to the establishment of an international monetary policy for the post-war period.
So that, Mr. Speaker, I submit that plans are well advanced; that the groundwork has been laid for proposals which may be easily whipped into shape in preparation for the time when the war will be over. The meeting of dominion prime ministers in England only a few months ago was another conference which I think might be regarded as one more step to prepare for the post-war period. Therefore we have all this groundwork, both in our own country and abroad, with which we have been actively associated. In addition, every municipality, every city, every town and every hamlet have carried on studies and made plans for the period following the war. So that I believe we can say with some confidence that at least we know where we are going in this connection.
We are indeed a fortunate country. We enjoy a high standard of living, which was never so equitably distributed as at the present time. We have made and will continue to make progress, but in doing so we must help others. Some may fear that as we help others we may adversely affect our own standard of living. To those having this fear I commend the words uttered by President Roosevelt some time ago, when he said that as we help raise the standard of living of other people we help raise our own standard of living as well. When one views the international post-war plans now being developed one cannot help feeling that a realistic approach is being made. Let us hope that nothing will occur to offset the plans already so well advanced' in the direction of carrying out the ideals of the Atlantic charter. Looking to this post-war period; approaching it with all the sincerity at my command, to me there is only one man in the public life of Canada possessing the experience, the capacity, the understanding, the contacts and the approach which will be required of the person representing this country at the peace conference when that time arrives. That man is none other than our own Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Therefore I say that Canada will do well to bear in mind the period following this war, because whatever is done at the peace conference will have a lasting effect upon the world, and upon Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir), who has just taken his seat, on his eloquent confession of faith in his party and his government. I am quite sure his belief that the public still have confidence in that party, in the light of what has been taking place during the last two years, must be very reassuring to his colleagues on the other side of the house. I shall not say anything to shake that confidence.
The point of view of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party has already been set forth in this debate by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and other members of this group. By way of general observation I want to say that it is quite evident from the budget that this government still pins its faith upon our present monopoly, capitalist system, and that where the government has entered the field of public ownership it has done so reluctantly and as a war measure. Quite evidently it is the intention of the government to withdraw from this field, once the war is over, just as quickly as conditions permit. When you accept and recognize that position the budget becomes intelligible and is probably as progressive as could be expected, having those objectives in view. This much is certain, that if we are to fall back upon private enterprise to maintain production and keep up our national income, to provide employment and mass purchasing power after the war, we must give this enterprise whatever concessions are necessary to-enable it to do that job with adequate profit to capital.
I regret that the budget contains no reference to the broad field of education. I should like to urge upon the members of the cabinet that when the dominion-provincial conference, to which reference is made in the budget, is convened, educationists and education officials be given a place at that conference and that an arrangement be made under which the government may take some steps to deal with; the general subject of education in this country.
I should like to confine myr remarks to-night to two subjects mentioned in the budget, mining and oil. At page 4183 of Hansard the minister points out:
The government has very much in mind the need of a comprehensive and many-sided programme to encourage the efficient development of our natural resources and to assure that these-industries will make the maximum contribution to the expansion of employment, national income and national wealth after the war.
It is quite evident that private enterprise, as evidenced in the field of mining, and in the oil fields, has failed to meet the needs of the-
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy

nation, in war time. It is quite apparent that, by various measures, the government has had to come to the assistance of those enterprises, by tax relief and other concessions. All are agreed, I think, that some important changes are needed, if those industries are to function in the future.
The minister also indicates that this subject will be reviewed at the coming dominion-provincial conference. In the budget certain concessions are made to the mining interests. Already new companies enjoy a three-year exemption from excess profits tax. Last year's budget made a provision whereby mining companies may write off exploration and prospecting expenses incurred while prospecting anywhere in Canada for base or strategic minerals. This is extended for another year by the present budget.
Undoubtedly the changes in income and excess profits tax will also benefit the mining companies. Then, one-half the expenditures on maintenance and repairs now to be charged back to the income of previous fiscal periods, may also be used to assist the mining companies, since they may include underground development work as part of their maintenance costs. I presume also that the concessions in the budget with respect to research will benefit the mining industry.
Even these concessions do not meet the requests of those interested in mining, and particularly those interested in the purchase and sale of mining stock. They are asking for much more than these concessions indicate. They ask that the depletion allowance be raised from 33J per cent to 50 per cent of the net earnings of metal and industrial mineral mines. They want the taxes paid annually to provincial and municipal governments to be allowed as a deduction from the earnings of all mining companies, before assessment for dominion income or excess profits tax purposes. They want also that all annual expenditures made by mining companies on outside explorations in any part of Canada, except cost of options or the purchase of property, be allowed as deductions from earnings before assessment for dominion income and/or excess profits tax.
The hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) has ably set forth the case for the mining companies, and the claims which have been put forth in various briefs by organizations interested in mining. I think all hon. members recognize the importance of mining in the national economy. We are all anxious that in the post-war period the mining industry, and other natural resources of this country, should be developed in the interests of the people of Canada. Doubtless drastic changes are needed.

There are, however, other factors which have to be taken into consideration, and which should be considered by the dominion provincial conference, when it sets forth the new conditions under which mining is to be conducted. Let it not be forgotten that it is not the prospector of whom we have heard so much in the house, who usually profits from his discovery of mining claims or minerals. Usually he is the one who profits least from the discoveries he makes. Let us also remember that in many instances those who derive the most profit from the mining industry are those who manipulate the mining stock market, and who make little if any contribution to the actual development of our natural resources.
Again I think we should keep in mind the fact that we have no assurance, when the government has come to the assistance of mining companies, by way of tax concessions and various other means, that when those mining companies reach a profitable stage of development the profits accruing therefrom may not revert to a very few individuals, and the general public profit but very little.
There is another point which should be considered. Even to-day, with all our drastic tax regulations, it is still possible for those who are interested in mining to secure properties from prospectors, organize stock companies, unload the stock on the public and make profit therefrom, while their profits from that field go untaxed, since they are considered as capital increase, and not profit. That is a very broad field which has not yet been touched by our tax collectors. I think it would be well to consider what has happened in respect of one very successful mining company which in its 1943 report has complained of high taxes, shortage of manpower, the high cost of labour and decrease in profits. Let us review its history, briefly.
I refer particularly to the Lake Shore mines. This mine was incorporated in 1914, and began milling operations in 1918. The property is in the Kirkland lake area. In 1933 it obtained control over Kirkland, Hudson bay claims, Minnaker, and Kirkland claims. Its operations have been extremely profitable, as I shall show from figures taken from the Financial Corporation Analysis for October 11, 1943. This company when incorporated was authorized to issue and did issue 2,000,000 shares of stock at a par value of $1 a share. On this 82,000,000 capitalization the company has paid dividends and bonuses totalling 890,420,000 or $45.21 a share of a par value of SI. Since 1918, that is to say, every dollar

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy
[DOT]originally invested has earned $45.21 a share, or an average yearly return of $1.80, or 180 per cent, on the original investment.
Dividends and bonuses reached their peak in the depression years. Dividends reached $6 per share, or 600 per cent on the original investment in 1937, and $5 per share, or 500 per cent in 1938. In the banking and commerce committee we have been giving the bankers a Tather rough ride for having paid dividends amounting at one time to sixteen per cent, but in the light of this 600 per cent the bankers are novices compared with these men as financiers.

speechtext:
Would the hon. member
permit a question?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Surely.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In view of what the hon.
member has just stated, the great profits of one particular mining company, would it not be fair for him to mention some other mines in which there have been great losses, because if the government went into it they would have to absorb those large private enterprises and stand the losses. I would like the hon. member to give us an answer to that.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The point I am
making here is that when the government has made tax concessions, when it has come to the assistance of the mines in order to bring them to the stage of development, there is no evidence that the public is going to profit by reason of the government's investment. On the contrary, the likelihood is that the government will bear the expenses of those mines that are unprofitable, while those that are profitable will pass their profits on to a very few individuals.
Even if we base those dividends on the book value rather than on the par value of the stock the payments are still exorbitant. In terms of book value they range from 149 per cent in 1939 to 35 per cent in 1943. The tremendous dividends paid on the stock have raised and maintained its market value at fantastic levels. This stock which sold originally at $1 par value reached a high of $62 in 1936. It was never lower than $16. It was $16 in 1926 and is back again near that price at the present time. Despite the tremendous aggregate of $90,420,000, the capitalization remained unchanged at $2,000,000, and the concern has remained relatively small. Its total assets in 1939 were valued at $8,066,358, and in that year it paid in dividends $8,000,000. In other words, it paid in dividends almost as much as its total assets were valued at. The company has unquestionably exploited the natural resources
and has paid out tremendous dividends totalling many times the original investment. Little has been set aside for depreciation. Surpluses above dividends have been valued at considerably more than the total capitalization, and in some years, for instance in 1939, 1940 and 1941, the company paid part of its huge dividends out of its accumulated surplus.
Mining interests are asking the government to raise the ante on depletion exemptions, to exempt depletions up to fifty per cent. Here was a very successful mine which depreciated its own surplus in order to pay out dividends, the depletions being from $1,278,129 in 1939 to $198,682 in 1941. Yet these are the people who come to the government asking that a greater allowance be made for depletion. In other words, instead of the surplus earnings from this company being used to any extent to finance an expansion of operations so as to increase total output, they have been dissipated in the form of large dividends and bonuses to stockholders.
The total value of assets, gross earnings, net income and dividend (payments from Lake Shore Mines has been falling steadily since the war began, and taxes have declined correspondingly. The dividend rate, however, has remained substantial. Even the eighty cents per share rate or $1,600,000 in total dividends and bonuses in 1043 represents a return of thirty-five per cent on the book value of the stock as of that year and more than twemty-two per cent of the total assets of the company.
As I have pointed out, in 1939 the dividends totalled $8,000,000, or almost the equivalent of the entire value of the total assets of that year. Despite this phenomenal record of earnings, perhaps because of their dissipation in huge dividends and bonuses, the company reported difficulty in maintaining operations. In its annual report for 1932 it complained that:
The war has made it necessary to tax the income of mines far beyond the point wdiere they can expand or even long exist.
This statement, in the light of the record of this company, and as made by this company, is simply ridiculous. In 1943 their report points to other difficulties: The labour strike in 1941-42, the growing man-power shortage in wartime, the growing degree of "rockburst" due to greater depth of operations, have all reduced the tonnage of ore processed and thus reduced earnings. But "in the meantime," the report states:
. . . operations continue to show a good profit, ore reserves developed ahead of mill requirements are adequate, results of new deep levels carry considerable promise, and the company's
The Budget-Mr. Noseioorthy

financial position remains strong, with the present dividend rate of 20 cents quarterly fairly well protected with current earnings.
As regards the tax policy of the future, this company's record, at least on the face of it, would justify maintaining the present excess profits tax and maldng no allowances for depreciation and expansion. It has earned enough to finance many times more expansion than it has ever undertaken, even in war years. Tax concessions in this case would merely fatten the net income of the concern and enable it to pay even more fantastic dividends. It raises the question as to what extent can we depend upon the profit motive to provide socially useful expansion in our mining area.
Another industry about which the government has becomq very solicitous, an industry to whose assistance the government has had to come in war time, is the oil industry. In the light of the fact that one company, the Imperial Oil company, controls fifty per cent or more of our supply, and was recognized by the Stevens committee as being the company which fixed the price for other companies, and inasmuch as this company is about seventy per cent owned by Standard Oil, it is well to look into its earnings, as an enterprise to which we have made such concessions in the Northwest Territories, before we begin making too many more government concessions. I have not time to go fully into the history of this company. It is an example of a corporation which has grown tremendously, has financed its own rapidly expanding operations and has built up a large capitalization almost exclusively through ploughing back its surplus profits into its business.
The original number of $100 par shares was doubled in 1915 with a 100 per cent stock dividend, and has been increased sixty-four times since then by three four-to-one splits in the stock. So that for every $100 par share originally held, there now exist 128 shares of no par value whose book value is $5.80 a share and whose present stock value was quoted yesterday at $14.50 a share. In other words'; for every $100 invested in the original company there is now $1,856 in stock. The original capital investment of $10 million has grown to about $40 million by other issues of stock. To-day the total assets are given at $181,250,000. In addition to the splits in stock, shareholders were able to get additional purchases of shares at especially favourable prices. The dividends paid on these shares have been very substantial. The par value of the shares was $25 up to 1924. In 1925 they were split four wa3rs, giving them a nominal value of $6.25 each. On this $6.25 nominal par value

dividends per share were paid as follows: in 1925, $1, or fourteen per cent; in 1926, $1.25, or twenty per cent; in 1927, $1.50, or twenty-five per cent; the same in 1928. In 1929 the stock was again split four ways, giving a nominal par value of about $1.56 a share. On this basis the shares paid dividends as follows:
1929,	87^ cents, or practically fifty per cent;
1930,	$1, or sixty-six per cent; 1931 to 1933, fifty cents, or thirty-three per cent; 1934; 92J cents, or sixty per cent; 1935 to 1938, $1.25, or eighty per cent; 1939, $1, or sixty-six per cent; 1940, 62J cents, or forty per cent; 1941 to 1943, fifty cents, or thirty-three per cent. In other words, there was continual splitting and multiplication of stock during the boom days of the twenties, and on this split and multiplied stock, earnings per share remained the same during the nineteen-thirties. Since the outbreak of the war this has been reduced slightly but still is exorbitant in terms of what the stockholder has put into the concern.
Those are the companies which are to-day crying for government assistance, for remission of taxation, companies to whose assistance the government has had to come in order to meet the war needs of the nation. Certainly a situation of that kind provokes the question raised by the minister in his budget speech, that of the need of some radical change being introduced if those industries are to function in the interests of all the people of Canada, instead of functioning, where successful, in the interests of a comparatively small group of shareholders. Hon. members opposite and to our right may disagree with the policy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in relation to those companies; but disagree as you will, I think we have to face the fact that neither in peace time nor in war has the development of our natural resources, as it has been carried out in the past, met the basic needs of the people of Canada, so that some means whereby that development can be brought into line with the needs of the country must be found by whatever party takes government in Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In taking part in this debate I wish first to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) upon the able way in which he delivered the budget. The budget this year is of great magnitude, which I would say was contemplated by all serious thinking Canadians, though those who want to play politics will find faults in it. This would be expected in peace time, but surely not in war time and especially at this crucial moment when our forces, along with those of the allied nations, are in the most desperate struggle the world has ever known.

The Budget-Mr. Leger
We are, one would say, at the cross-roads in the battle of freedom and democracy. The Canadian people in general want this government to supply the armed forces with all the best equipment that money can buy. In these modern times science has developed so many instruments of destruction which are very costly, but they must be supplied in order to beat down the forces of evil who are attacking us.
We are winning the war, but more gruesome days are still to come. Evil has never won over righteousness. The supreme power is on our side, and for this reason we shall win, so that the four freedoms of the Atlantic charter may be obtained. The Canadian people have done a great job so far and will keep on doing so until the war is won. Industry has produced beyond our imagination. Our farmers and fishermen have produced more than at any other time in our history, with much less manpower, which means that they have worked harder and longer hours. They have done so and will do so to the end of hostilities. There are certain regulations which had to be passed in order to stop inflation and they do not suit many of us; but it must be realized that they were passed for the general welfare of our people. Canada was asked, along with the Americans, to feed most of the allied nations, and as the war progresses they are being asked to feed the nations that we are liberating.
Canada has a big job to do and will do it, because all the Canadian people understand and know the hardships, the sacrifices, the torture and the humiliation which the European peoples have had to endure in the last four years. One must also take into consideration the destruction which has occurred and which is taking place at present in England, in North Africa, in Russia and all over Europe. We in Canada have until now been very fortunate, so much so that some Canadians- thank God only a small group-do not realize the seriousness of the war and are prepared to criticize the restrictions which had to be passed.
During this session the government has established a reconstruction department whose duty it will be to provide work, to launch public programmes, to develop more natural resources, to turn every war-time plant into a peace-time industry, and to provide certain facilities to our maritime farmers and fishermen, as well as to meet certain needs of the western provinces. The farmers of New Brunswick, especially in my riding of Kent, are in need of warehouses and cold storage facilities so that the farmers may keep and sell their produce in groups rather than individually. The fishermen of Kent county as well as of the maritimes generally need quick-freezing
plants at certain points in each county so that their fish will be quickly frozen, and as soon as possible after it is caught. In this way the fish will maintain the good flavour which it has when eaten fresh, and the people of the central provinces will then appreciate our different varieties of fish caught in the salt waters of the maritimes, the flavour of which is so superior compared with that of fresh water fish.
Candidly, I believe that the Minister of Finance should carefully consider these suggestions with the new Minister of Reconstruction and have them become realities after the war. A programme of decentralization of industry should be embarked upon as soon as possible. We . should undertake the development of our natural resources in all Canada and not only in the central part of the dominion, and when I say the central part I mean Ontario and Quebec. We have in the maritimes, at Hopewell, New Brunswick, near Moncton, a great hydro possibility through the harnessing of the tidal water at the junction of the Memramcook and the Petit-codiac rivers. Both these rivers meet at one point to flow into the bay of Fundy. It is known that these rivers and the bay of Fundy have a great rise and fall, an average of forty feet twice in twenty-four hours in normal times, and as high as fifty-five feet in the spring at Hopewell.
I am glad to know that both the government of New Brunswick and the dominion are negotiating to have an accurate survey made of these possibilities. If this investigation proves the project feasible, we should embark upon the construction of it as soon as possible after the war, because this development would provide electric power as cheap as any place in Canada, thus inducing manufactures to establish in our province. Doctor Turnbull, a prominent engineer, has made a thorough study of the project and believes it is quite feasible and could produce electricity as cheap, if not cheaper, than any other hydro development in Canada.
We must also see to it that the national revenue is fairly distributed among all classes of the nation-especially the farmers and fishermen of the maritime provinces. Floor and ceiling prices must be established if we want to control the revenue so that it is fairly distributed among all classes. My reason for mentioning this at this time is that we all know that the Department of Finance plays a big role in all these ventures. The people of Canada and the world want these things to become a reality and the government will have to do something. We all know what happened to France with all her different
The Budget-Mr. FulforcL

parties; we are on the verge of the same reaction in Canada unless the Canadian people wake up to the fact that a government is the people of the nation, and the money it spends must come from the people in fhe form of direct or indirect taxes or loans. Let us imagine having some irresponsible or radical government handling Canada's affairs after the war. This would be disastrous for the future progress of Canada. It is a recognized fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is one of the outstanding political economists in the world to-day. Fortunately, the Canadian people are realistic and recognize very well that the future of Canada depends on the present Prime Minister remaining at the helm of the government, so that when the war is finished, he will be at the peace table looking after the interests of Canadians for generations yet to come.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Like the hon. members who have preceded me in this debate I wish at the beginning of my remarks to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) not only on this budget but on all preceding budgets that it has been his responsibility to introduce im this house. I know it is not a pleasant job to increase taxes year after year as the war progresses. Especially would that be disagreeable when he himself has to pay the very same taxes we and all the rest of Canada are asked to pay. This is total war, and that is our method of financing our share of the war. I believe Canada's contribution will go down in history as one of the most remarkable that any country with a small population has ever made in time of war. Surely the responsibilities and duties of the minister should not be made doubly hard by sniping at him from ambush, especially by members of his own party. It is indeed a load too much for any one man to carry.
The people of Canada have confidence in our minister. I do not believe that there is anybody in the government in whom they have more confidence; yet there are those in this house who condemn him for doing what he knows in his own mind is right, although at times it is the hard road for him to follow. Oh, it would have been a great thing if in this last budget taxes could have been substantially reduced. I am sure that nobody would have enjoyed reducing them more than the minister himself; but may I repeat, this is total war and the war is not yet won. The German army is showing signs of disintegration, but we get very little news of the morale of the country. If Germany does collapse this year, as we all reverently

hope and pray, we still have Japan to defeat and we still have the immediate post-war period which will require tremendous financing.
I believe that certain inequalities have been eliminated in this budget. I was particularly pleased that the tariff and the excise foreign exchange tax have been eliminated from farm machinery. In spite of what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) said this afternoon, there is no doubt that as soon as farm machinery is again available in large quantities farmers will have to renew a great deal of the machinery which is not only worn out but, in many instances, obsolete. During the years of depression many farmers were unable-to buy even repair parts. They had to resort to makeshift repairs by the local blacksmith shop or by themselves in order to keep their machinery together. As soon as the war is over, those machines will be renewed, and there will be a great saving to the farmers-who buy machinery not only in the vast prairies of our west but also in eastern. Canada.
I was also pleased to see the ten per cent, compulsory savings clause of the income tax act abolished. By the abolition of this feature of the act those who are wage-earners in the low income tax brackets will benefit the most and, as incomes increase, the saving will be increasingly smaller until the limit of SI,200 is reached. In many instances this compulsory saving was never paid owing to the offset of insurance policies and other methods of -saving effected by those who could afford to do so.
Representing as I do a riding which is partly agricultural and partly industrial I heartily commend the minister for the two reductions which have been effected in this budget. I am very keen on having a floor maintained after the war under agricultural prices. Never again do I want to see the farmers of my riding, which is one of Canada's greatest dairying: counties, having to accept sixty-five cents a hundredweight for milk. To-day they are receiving roughly $2 a hundredweight, which is a fair return for their labour and capital investment. I believe that by long term agreements with Great Britain and reciprocal agreements with other nations throughout the world, Canadian farm products can be sold at established prices and our surpluses disposed of beyond the shores of this country.
I should like to speak yery briefly of small industries which before the war were working on a shoe-string, industries employing from six to twenty men or women. Some of these industries are engaged on war contracts, and

The Budget-Mr. Fuljord
consequently are allowed special depreciation, but I would say that by far the greater proportion have carried on as in peace time, or have received subcontracts from the larger war industries. Many of these concerns made such small profits before the war that they lived from hand to mouth. While they had the right to appear before a board of arbitration to decide what should be their normal profit, when the 100 per cent excess profits tax is collected, apart from the twenty per cent which is to be refunded after the war they will be left without reserves, and unless they are given special consideration I am afraid many of these industries will not be able to survive the period of readjustment.
It is my sincere belief that the vast majority of hon. members on all sides of this house are conscientiously endeavouring to improve the conditions of the common people. To be conscientious, however, one must be sincere and, above all, consistent. For that reason I was astounded at the remarks of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) as reported at page 4338 of Hansard:
I can well recall when the compulsory savings plan was adopted. Some may not have understood me when I said it was on this side of the house it was proposed, and it was on that side of the house compulsory savings were adopted. To-day they are disbanded. Why? It would seem that they are needed more now; they are needed more at the present time.
Now I turn to page 4346, where I find the amendment moved by the hon. member, and read paragraph (b);
that no effective action has been taken to grant a measure of relief to the men and women in the lower income brackets by raising the exemption in income tax for single persons to not less than $800 per annum and for married persons to not less than $1,600 per annum.
I do not think anything could be more inconsistent, more completely contradictory than those two statements. I also believe that our hon. friends opposite must be pretty hard pressed for arguments when the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) should have to devote the greater part of his speech to a criticism of the man-power policy of the government. It is true that our man-power policy is not perfect, but I venture to say that one of the matters most criticized in any democratic countries constituting the united nations is the very point dealt with by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I know you seldom pick up a United States newspaper without reading some article or the report of some speech condemning the United States selective service system, in spite of the fact that the United States has had conscription for overseas service since the outbreak of war. To
me it is a revelation that Canada, a country with a small population, should be able to produce so much. It is true that we have a vast store of natural resources, but if our man-power policy had been completely at fault we never would have been able to attain the position Canada occupies to-day, as the fourth largest producer amongst the united nations.
Since coming to this house I have followed as closely as possible the arguments advanced day after day, week after week and month after month by the Social Credit party, but I am still in the dark as to just what their members propose. If they can solve the problem of distribution after the war, I say, more power to them, but certainly I have not heard anything from that corner of the house to lead me to believe they will be able to do so. If they could do away with the old vicious circle which is characterized by the man planting corn to raise pigs to kill pigs to make fertilizer to grow corn, then they would accomplish a great deal, but I doubt if we shall ever see that vicious circle again.
The policies of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation should be clear as crystal, but somehow they are not. To me they are a potpourri of socialism and. if I may use a modern slang expression, double talk. I have found it impossible to get anything but evasive answers to pertinent questions. I have yet to hear the leader of the C.C.F. party, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), definitely state what is meant by the conscription of capital. By that does he mean the conscription of savings accounts, or life insurance policies or war savings stamps or bonds? How much of it or would all be conscripted? Nothing but evasion has ever been given to that question. In fact, I find that asking members of the C.C.F party for a definite answ'er is like trying to nail a piece of jelly to the wall: it just does not nail.
On one hand we hear private monopolies condemned, while on the other hand, according to the logic of the C.C.F., they would create the greatest monopoly of all, namely complete government ownership. They decry the capitalistic system, the system under which Canada has built up one of the highest standards of living in the world. I believe that our standard of living is exceeded only by that in the United States, which, incidentally, is also a capitalistic country.
Actually the whole world was in turmoil before the world war. There was greed and suspicion instead of determination and understanding among members of the League of Nations. Here are but a few factors the C.C.F. omit to mention when referring to the depres-
The Budget-Mr. Fuljord

sion, one of the world's worst depressions, which occurred in the decade preceding this war.
First of all, we must go back to the stock market crash in 1929. From 1926 to 1929, everyone who could scrape up a few dollars plunged into the stock market, in an attempt to get money without working. Stenographers in offices, filing clerks, yes, even office boys would spend their lunch hours in brokerage offices, watching the prices of various shares as they appeared on the ticker tape. This was one of the most glaring examples of inflation that one could imagine. Certain stocks rose to unheard of heights, even after commodity prices had started to break.
Naturally, deflation set in, and overnight, in October, 1929, millions were wiped out. Certain regulations have since been put into effect which, I believe, will eliminate any such wild orgy as we saw on the stock market between 1926 and 1929.
In the early thirties Russia was completing its first five-year plan, and was beginning its second five-year plan; the grain markets of the world were flooded by Russian grain, particularly Russian wheat. I am not condemning Russia for taking this action. I happened to be in Russia in 1931, and I saw people going without the bare necessities of life in order to sell this grain abroad, so that they could acquire the necessary foreign exchange and foreign gold with which to buy the machinery to start their industrial development. Had they not made that sacrifice, I do not believe the Russian people would have been able to throw back the German hordes as they did at the gates of Moscow, and as they did from the very heart of Stalingrad. It was through that sacrifice that Russia came out on top. Nevertheless, the fact remains that Russia undersold the world's grain markets, and farmers in the Canadian west had to suffer.
Then, let us consider the accumulation of gold in the United States at that time. That gold was sent to pay for war debts owed to that country, and it was promptly buried at Fort Knox, Kentucky. No one realizes mistakes to-day more than does the United States.
One of the problems which must be faced and solved at the monetary conference taking place at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, will be to find methods of using this gold, so as to create credit in those countries that have felt the oppression of the nazis, and those countries which will have to be rebuilt from the ground up, financially and economically, after the war.

We must remember, too, the war of tariffs which began and continued throughout the thirties. Each country thought it could live unto itself. We know that after this war no country can live unto itself; no country can dominate the rest of the world. We must learn to believe each other, to help each other and to develop a league of nations which will really function, a league of nations in which countries will respect and trust one another.
We remember, too, the growth of fascism, which started in Italy. That belief rapidly spread to Japan. We must remember, too, that Japan was the first country to take action in this war, when she marched into Manchuria in 1931. At the same time Japan was flooding the world with cheap goods. All hon. members will remember electric light bulbs made in Japan which burnt out the very first time they were placed in a socket. At the same time Germany undersold the world in heavy machinery and manipulated her foreign exchange in such a way as to get gold to purchase the essentials to manufacture war materials. Germany then took back the Ruhr, and Italy marched into Ethiopia.
All these factors contributed to the world depression-not the capitalistic system. We shall recall, too, the anschluss in Austria, the Munich conference, with the whole world upset. We remember the carving up of Czechoslovakia, with the result that the world was in a maelstrom of uncertainty.
As a final result, war broke out. But war will not always last. Canada can come out on the top, if we hold our heads after the war. We shall come out on top if we retain those sound financial policies set forth by our Minister of Finance, and if we carry along on the road laid by him. We owe it to those who are overseas that the Canada to which they will come back will be on a sound basis financially and economically, not a Canada in which a group of inexperienced experimenters are trying to run the country.
On motion of Mr. Ralston the debate was adjourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
